fullText:
The Athletics have parted ways with former general manager David Forst after a season in which the team has struggled to win games.

With a 45-70 record this season, the Athletics have been one of the biggest disappointments in all of MLB. Armed with a load of young, talented, and controllable players, things have seemingly fallen apart for the Athletics, who were supposed to contend for the playoffs this season. Instead, the team is battling the Los Angeles Angels for last place in the American League West, and it cost Forst his job.

The Athletics confirmed in a statement that they have parted ways with Forst, with assistant general manager Dan Feinstein taking over on an interim basis for the rest of 2026.

"David has been an integral part of the A's and our success for nearly three decades. His leadership, dedication, and commitment to this team have helped shape our baseball operations department and position us for the future. We are grateful for everything David has done for our organization," said A's owner and managing partner John Fisher in a statement posted on the team's website.

Forst also spoke after leaving the team that he has spent the last 27 years with, offering a classy statement after exiting the organization.

"It was truly an honor to spend the last 27 years with the A's, especially the last 11 as the GM. This organization is full of incredibly talented, devoted, and good people, and I am lucky to have worked alongside them for so long," Forst said.

The 50-year-old Forst was first hired by the A's in 2000, when he worked as a scout for the team. He then became the team's assistant general manager to Billy Beane in 2004 and was then promoted to general manager in 2015 after Beane left his post.

The Athletics won the AL West just once during Forst's 10 seasons as the team's GM, in 2020, and only made the playoffs three times.

With the team slated to move to Las Vegas for 2028, they will have a new front office in place.

title: 49ers rookie earns great nickname from QB Mac Jones
description: De'Zhaun Stribling continues to gain praise in his first offseason with the 49ers.
fullText:
De'Zhaun Stribling has only been a member of the San Francisco 49ers since April, but he's already earned a nickname from the veteran in the quarterback room

"I call him 'The Flying Hawaiian' because he's so fast," backup quarterback Mac Jones said. "But he definitely is fast, but some guys, you know, they can be really quick, but they're not as strong, so he has both. I don't have a comp for him yet, but I think he'll be a really good player."

"I call him the Flyin' Hawaiian because he's so fast." 

Mac Jones on #49ers rookie De'Zhaun Stribling. pic.twitter.com/9JYI8cRB0c

Stribling, who was born near Honolulu, Hawaiʻi, was the No. 33 overall pick in the second round of the 2026 NFL Draft by the 49ers. The wideout capped a five-year college journey that took him from Washington State to Oklahoma State before he landed at Ole Miss for his final season. In 2025, Stribling caught 55 passes for 811 yards and six touchdowns for the Rebels, and he ran a 4.36-second 40-yard dash at the Combine to go with a 36-inch vertical.

Where Stribling lands on the depth chart is still taking shape. With Ricky Pearsall sidelined for the entire 2026 season, the rookie looks like the No. 2 or No. 3 receiver behind Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel, and he's in a battle with Christian Kirk for reps as San Francisco sorts out its post-Pearsall pecking order.

Jones likely won't be the one throwing Stribling the ball much once the season starts, barring another injury to Brock Purdy. But the backup quarterback has become a well-liked figure in that quarterback room and around the building after the role he played a year ago, when he went 5-3 as a starter and helped steer the 49ers into the playoffs while Purdy worked through a turf toe injury.

Stribling has been gaining hype all offseason, and praise continues to trickle down to the rest of the team as the regular season draws nearer.

title: Broncos DL Matt Henningsen suffered a torn Achilles
description: One year ago, on August 7th of 2025, Denver Broncos defensive lineman Matt Henningsen suffered a season-ending Achilles injury. A brutal injury that can end the careers of some players. Henningsen rehabbed, was re-signed by the Broncos, and was able to get back on the practice field and be ready for training camp. Not only […]
fullText:
One year ago, on August 7th of 2025, Denver Broncos defensive lineman Matt Henningsen suffered a season-ending Achilles injury. A brutal injury that can end the careers of some players. Henningsen rehabbed, was re-signed by the Broncos, and was able to get back on the practice field and be ready for training camp. Not only did he return to the field, but he has been a standout player for the Broncos' second- and third-team defensive line and was making a case for a 53-man roster spot.

Unfortunately, the universe just has it out for Henningsen because exactly one year from his previous Achilles injury, Matt Henningsen went down early in practice and had to be carted off the field. The injury did not look good, and a few moments ago, 9NEWS Denver's Mike Klis confirmed those fears when he reported that Henningsen suffered an Achilles injury.

Devastating news: #Broncos DL Matt Henningsen suffered a torn Achilles today per source. It occurred one year after he tore his other Achilles during joint practice with 49ers in Santa Clara.
All that rehab. All that work to come back. And Henningsen was having a good camp.

Henningsen was a 6th-round selection for the Denver Broncos back in the 2022 NFL Draft and became an instant contributor for them in the middle of their defense. He would appear in 34 games for the Broncos between 2022 and 2023 before spending the 2024 season on the team's practice squad. He looked like a strong candidate for a practice squad spot last year before the Achilles injury and was once again making a case for a spot on the team this year, but unfortunately, the Achilles injury got him again.

It's tough to ignore the coincidences here. The same injury, to the same player, exactly one year apart. Absolutely devastating for Henningsen. This will unfortunately put his NFL future in limbo moving forward as well. He re-signed with the team on a one-year deal this offseason, so we'll see if the team will bring him back again or not.

This is also a hit to the Broncos' defensive line depth. Henningsen was one of their top reserve/depth players, and now he is done for the year for a second straight season. I would look for the Broncos to bring in some depth, especially before their preseason opener next week, since veterans like DJ Jones, Zach Allen, and Malcolm Roach are not expected to play much, if at all.

The injury bug has bitten the Broncos early in training camp, but thankfully they have been mostly minor thus far. Henningsen's injury changes that, and hopefully Marvin Mims and Nate Adkins, who both left practice as well, only suffered minor injuries.

title: Today in sports history, August 6

1890: Cy Young made his major league debut and pitched a three-hitter as the Cleveland Spiders defeated the Chicago Colts. He ended his career with a record 511 victories.

1972: Gary Player captured the PGA Championship, winning the tournament by two strokes for the second PGA title of his career.

1972: Atlanta Braves star Hank Aaron hit his 660th career home run, surpassing Babe Ruth's record of 659 homers with one franchise, then homered again in the 10th inning to beat Cincinnati.

1973: Roberto Clemente and Warren Spahn were inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Clemente became the first Latin American player enshrined, while Spahn entered with the most career victories by a left-handed pitcher.

1978: John Mahaffey overcame a seven-stroke final-round deficit and defeated Tom Watson and Jerry Pate on the second sudden-death hole to win the PGA Championship at Oakmont.

1988: José Canseco became just the 11th player in major league history to record a 30-home run, 30-stolen base season.

1988: Goose Gossage recorded the 300th save of his career, becoming only the second pitcher in major league history to reach the milestone.

1992: Kevin Young won the Olympic 400-meter hurdles in a world-record 46.78 seconds in Barcelona, becoming the first man to break 47 seconds in the event.

1999: San Diego Padres star Tony Gwynn collected his 3,000th career hit with a first-inning single against the Montreal Expos and finished with four hits in a 12-10 victory.

2022: Tony Boselli, Cliff Branch, LeRoy Butler, Art McNally, Sam Mills, Richard Seymour, Dick Vermeil and Bryant Young were inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

2024: American Cole Hocker surged past Josh Kerr and Jakob Ingebrigtsen to win the Olympic 1,500 meters in an Olympic-record 3:27.65 in Paris.

title: Giants Get Cam Skattebo Injury Scare at Training Camp

fullText:
The New York Giants faced a bit of a scare at Friday's training camp practice when several players got banged up during live scrimmages and drills, including second-year running back Cam Skattebo.

ESPN's Jordan Raanan, who is in attendance at camp in West Virginia, shared details on Skattebo, center John Michael Schmitz, and edge Brian Burns.

"RB Cam Skattebo went down after a collision with LB Arvell Reese. He was stretching his left leg and didn't return to practice but remained on sideline," wrote Raanan.

"C John Michael Schmitz walked off early in practice after taking hard hit. OLB Brian Burns also got banged up but didn't appear serious."

While you never want to see players get hurt, especially before the season even begins, Giants fans can take a deep breath as it appears all of the aforementioned players will be okay.

After practice, New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh gave a brief update on Skattebo, Schmitz, and Burns, and reiterated that nobody was seriously harmed at Friday's practice.

"John Harbaugh said JMS hit his head/got his bell rung. Skattebo just part of working back from last year's injury but nothing serious. Brian Burns played some but is managing an ankle," wrote the New York Daily News' Pat Leonard.

It's certainly a good update that no Giant will be missing any major practice time in the coming weeks, as all three players will be key starters for New York in 2026.

Skattebo in particular seems to still be getting reacclimated to the speed of the NFL. After all, he missed the second half of his rookie season and will likely need some reps throughout camp and the preseason to be 100% ready for Week 1.

If there's one positive thing New York Giants fans can take away from Skattebo's near-injury, it's the fact that it came on a monstrous play from first-round rookie Arvell Reese.

NorthJersey.com's Art Stapleton detailed the series of events in a post on X.

"Arvell Reese is the total package. Brings it old school. Popped Cam Skattebo in a run fit + the oohs/aahs were audible," wrote Stapleton.

"Next play Reese ran down Skatt from back side behind line. Skatt was slow to get up. Did a lot of stretching on side before walking across to other sideline."

One constant throughout Giants training camp thus far has been the emergence of Reese and how fast he seems to be adapting to the high-level of the NFL.

The fifth overall pick in this past April's draft, the former Ohio State standout figures to wear multiple hats for the Giants defense this upcoming season.

It seems he'll primarily serve as a weakside linebacker, serving as the sidekick to Tremaine Edmunds.

But thanks to his special physical abilities, there will be instances where new defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson will be able to send him as a pass rusher, an area he thrived at in college.

Let's just hope he refrains from laying the boom on any more Giants teammates.

title: Senators Shut Out Of NHL Network's Top 20 Winger Rankings
description: The one Senators winger who managed to crack NHL Network's top 20 now plays somewhere else.
fullText:
As the Senators prepare for a new season, they're a team with good depth at forward, but when it comes to elite wingers, they're a little shy on those.

NHL Network recently unveiled its ranking of the league's top 20 wingers entering the 2026-27 season, and not a single current Senator made the cut.

Well, technically, there is one familiar face.

Steve Warne and Gregg Kennedy discuss Travis Green's recent comments on Brady Tkachuk's exit.

Brady Tkachuk checks in at No. 18, but in Ottawa, he's nobody's concern after being traded to the Florida Panthers in June.

Beyond Tkachuk, whom Sens fans would happily argue against, they don't really have an elite winger right now they could argue for.

Nikita Kucherov tops the NHL list, followed by David Pastrnak, Kirill Kaprizov, Mitch Marner and Mikko Rantanen. Matt Boldy, Jason Robertson, Matthew Tkachuk, Cole Caufield and William Nylander round out the top 10.

In other words, it's basically an All-Star lineup.

And that's the problem for the Senators. They do have a deep stable of solid wingers, but it's difficult to make a convincing case that any of them belongs in that company right now.

That's why so many fans are clamouring for more help in the top six,

Drake Batherson is probably Ottawa's best established winger these days. He's been one of the club's most consistent offensive producers and remains an important part of that top six.

But would he look a little out of place on this list?

Lucas Raymond grabbed the final spot at No. 20 after putting up 76 points for Detroit last season. Just ahead of him is Anaheim's Cutter Gauthier, who exploded for 41 goals. Tkachuk is 18th, followed by Utah's Clayton Keller and Tampa Bay's Jake Guentzel.

That's a pretty high bar just to get into the conversation.

Batherson is certainly capable of pushing closer to that level. But as things stand today, it would be tough to flick any of those players off the list to make room for him.

William Eklund is intriguing. As a former 7th overall pick, he has pedigree, and at 23, he still has time to grow. Perhaps he's the one guy who might have a chance to force his way into this type of discussion.

Veteran Claude Giroux once would have made a list like this. But he'll be 39 in January, so age has taken him out of contention.

And after them, the Senators don't have a single winger who even reached 40 points last season, let alone be thought of as a top 20 guy. The only guy who did just bailed on them.

So the Senators will have to settle for their good team depth at winger over individual excellence. And since it is a team game and always has been, that's not a bad thing.

Just ask the defending champion Carolina Hurricanes, who didn't register a single winger on this list either.

title: Giants HC John Harbaugh provides update after Cam Skattebo’s injury scare
description: New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh doesn't believe Cam Skattebo's injury scare is a serious situation.

New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo suffered an injury scare during training camp after colliding with linebacker Arvell Reese during practice. While it's a situation the club is monitoring, it doesn't sound like John Harbaugh is too concerned about it.

The 63-year-old head coach downplayed the injury completely when asked about it," according to Darryl Slater of NJ.com. Harbaugh claims Skattebo is not dealing with a serious injury and that the former fourth-round pick is currently working his way back from the severe lower-body injury he suffered midway through last season. From the sounds of it, Cam Skattebo is going through the motions of his injury recovery.

"After Friday's training camp practice, Giants coach John Harbaugh downplayed Cam Skattebo's apparent injury while speaking to reporters in West Virginia," Slater wrote. "Harbaugh said Skattebo isn't dealing with anything serious — and is just continuing to work his way back from last year's major ankle injury."

"He's probably working through the football shape part of it," Harbaugh said about Skattebo. "He's coming off of rehab, so that's what that was. It won't be a serious injury at all."

Skattebo flashed major potential in his first eight career games in the NFL. At one point, he became the Giants' go-to option in the offense before suffering an ankle dislocation, a fibula fracture, a tibia fracture, and a ruptured deltoid ligament in his right leg. title: Seahawks prep for Saturday Football Fest
description: We’re a little more than a week away from the Seahawks’ preseason opener against the Dallas Cowboys. Thursday, the team had to take practice inside because of the smoke. Saturday, they will pack Lumen Field for the “Seahawks’ Football Fest”.
fullText:
We're a little more than a week away from the Seahawks' preseason opener against the Dallas Cowboys.

Thursday, the team had to take practice inside because of the smoke. Saturday, they will pack Lumen Field for the "Seahawks' Football Fest".

The event is an evening of football, family, and fun. Featuring meet-and-greets, photo-ops with franchise legends, a live DJ, and team mascots.

Rashid Shaheed is going through his first training camp with the Hawks after joining the team midseason last year.

"I'm excited to see the energy of the fans," said the wide receiver. "It's going to be good to get back on home turf. And it's going to be a ton of good energy. We're all excited."

Tickets are still available, and they're about $17 each. A family-friendly way to enjoy the Seahawks up close before the season kicks off.

Gates open around 4:15 pm, and practice starts at 5:20 pm.

Plus, there'll be an autographed football toss around 7:20 pm.

However, while some of the younger players couldn't wait to get back in front of the 12's, one veteran admitted he was contemplating retirement this past offseason.

Linebacker Demarcus Lawrence said last year if the Hawks won it all, he'd hang up his cleats.

But, after a Super Bowl ring, as well as a discussion with his wife, he's said he's back for a 13th season. Eager to defend the championship he'd been chasing his whole career.

"With the type of team that we have…we should've been where we were last year," the veteran Linebacker calmly asserts.

"This is where the hard part begins, staying on top."

Lawrence admits winning the Lombardi Trophy was bittersweet. He says he couldn't walk away. He compared the situation to going from being the hunter chasing a goal to the hunted defending a title.

"They say it's no fun when the rabbit has the gun," Lawrence smirked.

"We're the ones with the dot on our back. So, I just want to see how that feels."

After spending his entire career with Dallas, Lawrence joined the Seahawks last offseason. He says the brotherhood on defense, especially with so many journeymen, is genuine.

"It's just great to have those caliber of leaders in the locker room with you. Like-minded guys."

That culture is on full display this year, thanks in part to HBO's Hard Knocks.

The training camp docuseries debuted earlier this week. And, Shaheed said everyone's hoping for a starring role.

"A ton of laughs, a ton of jokes. It's kind of cool to see how HBO portrays our team on TV," Shaheed said.

He says it's been a great insight into the mindset inside the building. A look at how the team competes against each other and how the franchise operates from top to bottom.

"I'm excited to continue to watch," says Shaheed.

title: For second year in a row, Astros missed on pitching at trade deadline. Can fragile rotation hold up?
description: Houston added Daulton Varsho but no pitching at the deadline. Now Ronel Blanco, Hayden Wesneski and Cristian Javier carry a fragile rotation.
fullText:
SAN DIEGO - Deterred by asking prices and optimistic about internal options, the Houston Astros did not augment their pitching staff before a trade deadline.

Those internal reinforcements did arrive, but their performance down the stretch underwhelmed, and it contributed to the Astros missing the playoffs.

That was last year. After this year's deadline unfolded similarly, with no additions on the pitching front, Houston's aspirations to return to the postseason may hinge on its tenuous rotation avoiding a reprise.

After making one deadline trade to acquire center fielder Daulton Varsho, general manager Dana Brown said last week the Astros "felt like we got close" in their pursuit of pitching help, but they made no deals there while weighing "what it's going to do to your prospect capital and the future of the organization."

JEFF BAGWELL: How Astros star fought alcoholism, got sober

It echoed a year ago, when the Astros balked at asking prices that were "too high" for pitching, as Brown said then, and focused on adding to their lineup. Erratic offense did prove arguably the main reason they missed the playoffs by a win, but the stretch run also illustrated the risk in their rotation approach.

Houston placed an onus on pitchers returning from surgeries - Cristian Javier and Luis Garcia, who were both coming back from Tommy John procedures; Spencer Arrighetti in his return from a thumb fracture; and for depth J.P. France returning from shoulder surgery - to fortify its major-league rotation.

Of that group, Javier alone remained in the rotation for the final two months and posted uneven results. Arrighetti made five starts before an elbow issue ended his season, Garcia made two starts before he re-injured his elbow and France returned late in the year for a brief appearance as a reliever.

Again, this year, the Astros are positioned to rely on two pitchers who just returned from elbow surgeries - Ronel Blanco and Hayden Wesneski - to hold rotation spots. Both are already taking regular turns, with little experienced depth behind them if any issues arise.

Wesneski's first two starts back have been encouraging. He has a 3.86 ERA and threw 5⅔ and 6 innings in them, despite totaling fewer than 80 pitches in both. Manager Joe Espada said after Wesneski's outing Tuesday he is keeping the right-hander around 80-85 pitches initially "before we can extend the leash."

"But his stuff is good, the velo is there, breaking pitches have the action that we're looking for," Espada said. "So he's checking all the boxes."

Blanco, slated to start Friday's opener against the Padres in his fourth start back, had a 7.36 ERA in his first three outings. He fell short of completing five innings in two of them, while allowing five home runs and eight walks in those 14⅔  innings.

Brown, in an appearance Wednesday on the Astros' flagship radio station 790 AM, voiced optimism that Blanco is "going to get back to the old Blanco." Brown also suggested, however, the Astros could "rotate him and (Tatsuya) Imai out at times, just to get him built back up."

"Once you come off these injuries, sometimes it's really tough to get your rhythm and consistency," said Brown. "So we'll monitor it closely with the (40-plus) games that we have left. But there's an opportunity that maybe we could put him in the pen for three or four innings, kind of like we're doing with Imai."

Since moving Imai to the bullpen last weekend, the Astros have remained vague about their plans for the right-hander down the stretch. Imai entered one game against Toronto in relief and worked three perfect innings. Espada said Tuesday that Imai was "being considered" for a start on this road trip.

Brown, in his radio appearance, said the Astros "feel like at some point (Imai)'ll be back in the rotation." Plugging him back in amid a playoff push would only magnify the pressure on Imai and the Astros' staff to rein in the inconsistency that has defined his first MLB season - and do so while the stakes increase.

Imai has cruised at times, but his tendency to derail early risks a toll on Houston's bullpen. If the plan is to rotate him back into occasional starts, having a stretched-out arm behind him could offer coverage - be it Blanco or someone else - but still carries uncertainty unless the Astros commit to a piggyback idea.

After his relief outing against the Blue Jays, Imai said he was alerted before the game he would likely be used after Javier ended his start and for multiple innings. The Astros trailed when he entered, however, leaving open the question of whether they would have handled the late innings differently with a lead.

Amid all of the rotation machinations, perhaps no pitcher has the chance to be more pivotal than Javier.

Javier, the highest-paid pitcher on Houston's roster, struggled in three starts before missing three months to a shoulder strain, then was stowed in the bullpen. He has a 6.59 ERA in 27⅓ innings, but his last two outings comprised five scoreless relief innings in Anaheim and a quality start against Toronto.

Only others' struggles have put Javier back in a position to start, yet none of the Astros' other options to fill out the rotation have his experience. Javier resembling his pre-surgery form could bolster the middle of the rotation behind Hunter Brown and Peter Lambert and ease the demand on the pitchers above.

The depth Dana Brown lauded this spring has dwindled. Trading Arrighetti for Varsho depleted it further, though Arrighetti was on the injured list. Mike Burrows is rehabbing from elbow neuritis, with no projected return date. Erstwhile starter Kai-Wei Teng is pitching as a reliever at Triple-A Sugar Land.

Houston just promoted pitching prospect Bryce Mayer to Triple-A, where he joins fellow prospect Ethan Pecko, forming perhaps a next wave of starting depth. Delving into it during a stretch run would double as an admission by the Astros of diminished faith in their options with major-league experience.

Entering Friday, the Astros still had the majors' third-highest rotation ERA. The group sported a 5.16 ERA since May 22, when Houston began a pivot from being 11 games under .500 to two games over with a 1-½ game division lead. Sustaining the latter, again, will fall to arms already in place.

There's more to Houston with the Chronicle.

title: Yankees, Braves announce new start time after rain delay
description: The Braves are in the Bronx, but so is bad weather.
fullText:
It's Unofficial 1990s Throwback Night at Yankee Stadium on Friday, as the Atlanta Braves are in town to face the Yankees for a three-game set.

These showdowns always bring to mind fond—for us anyway—memories of the 1996 and 1999 Fall Classics, when the Yankees came back from down 0-2 to win their first championship in 18 years and then when they polished off a similarly potent Braves team in a four-game sweep durig the final year of the 20th century (securing a repeat to follow the act of the legendary 1998 club). Of course, it's been many years since those rumbles, and from 2001 onward, the Yankees and Braves have the same number of titles: one apiece, in 2009 and 2021 respectively.

Tonight has a special sort of buzz about it, as erstwhile Braves ace Max Fried—who won the World Series clincher in Houston during that special 2021—will face his old team for the first time. The personnel has changed a bit since Fried departed after 2024 (including now-retired skipper Brian Snitker), but Ronald Acuña Jr., Ozzie Albies, Matt Olson, and plenty more are still around. Meanwhile, Atlanta will send out one of their Trade Deadline acquisitions, Tyler Mahle, who will make his Braves debut.

It'll be a fun showdown … whenever they get to play it. The weather in the Bronx is crummy at the moment and even though first pitch is still an hour away, the Yankees have announced that the game will not begin at 7:05pm ET as expected. Whenever the Yanks and MLB offer updates, we'll update our own article in turn. Stay dry and hang in there! The rain is supposed to subside, so we should get baseball tonight.

Please be advised we do not intend to start tonight’s game on time. Information will be provided as it is received.

Tonight’s first pitch is scheduled for approximately 9:00 PM.

Well, it took awhile, but we finally got an update. We'll see you in a little over 45 minutes for first pitch from Fried at 9pm ET.

title: Nets Ranked No. 12 Team in Eastern Conference, Too Low?
description: Despite adding star power in Julius Randle, Brooklyn sits near the bottom of the East. Explore why experts view Jordi Fernández’s squad as a dangerous dark horse.
fullText:
The Brooklyn Nets made some significant moves this offseason, adding a good mix of young and veteran talent to the roster.

On Friday, Michael Pina, senior staff writer at The Ringer, released a podcast where he ranked every team in the Eastern Conference.

The Nets came in at No. 12, beating out the Milwaukee Bucks, Chicago Bulls, and Washington Wizards.

Pina noted the dedication of the front office to head coach Jordi Fernández, who inked an extension this offseason despite a slow start to his head coaching career.

He said that Fernández is his "dark horse" candidate for Coach of the Year, while giving him credit for elevating Michael Porter Jr.'s game last season.

Porter had his best year as a pro in his first season with the Nets, averaging 24.2 points, 7.1 rebounds and a career-best three assists.

Following the end of the Nets' 20-win regular season, Porter told reporters in the team's season wrap-up press conference he wants to be a part of the Nets' turnaround.

"If it was up to me, I'd love to sign an extension with this franchise," Porter said. "I would love to spend many, many years in Brooklyn and make this my home and watch this franchise take off."

Entering the final year of his five-year, $179 million deal that he initially signed with the Denver Nuggets, it may be smart to lock down Porter before he increases his price tag.

Julius Randle was the biggest name acquired by Brooklyn this offseason, as the front office mad a move for the 3-time NBA All Star just one night before the draft.

Pina said that he was surprised by the move, but admitted that it could be the "perfect space" for a player like Randle, who needs the ball in his hands to be effective.

In his second season with the Minnesota Timberwolves, Randle scored 21.2 points per game, adding 6.7 rebounds and 5.1 assists on solid 48.1-percent shooting.

After a solid first round showing against the Nuggets, Randle struggled immensely against the San Antonio Spurs' length and size, which had many analysts and fans calling for Minnesota to look to move the 3-time All-Star.

Additions like Tyler Bilodeau and Moritz Wagner are big for helping Sharpe get acclimated, while the 1-2 punch of Mikel Brown Jr. and Egor Dëmin in the backcourt is intriguing.

Expect the Nets to make some noise as a potential play-in team this upcoming year.

title: Pirates Get Big Konnor Griffin Injury Update Amid Playoff Chase

fullText:
The 2026 season for the Pittsburgh Pirates has been one of ups and downs, with the team playing inconsistent baseball throughout.

Pittsburgh got off to a nice start, and the team was looking like it could finally end the long playoff drought. Adding in the emergence of its young stars, the Pirates have started to look like a force to deal with.

But over the last 10 games, the Pirates have gone 2-8, seeing themselves slip down the standings. Currently, the Pirates hold a record of 57-60 on the year, sitting in last place within the National League Central division.

While the division is likely out of the question, the race for a wild-card spot is still there. Pittsburgh is dealing with a crowded field in the NL race, but if the team can put together a few solid series over the next few weeks, it could set them up well.

The Pirates have been dealing with some injury concerns of late, leading to the struggles. One of which involves rookie sensation Konnor Griffin, who has been on the injured list for a month recovering from a torn left ring finger sagittal band.

The infielder has been recovering well, and the team will check in on him around mid-August to see how he's doing. If all goes well, Griffin will then go on a rehab assignment before he can return to the Pirates.

"It's getting better," Griffin said. "This is kind of like a broken bone. You've got to let it heal, so I'm not moving it much outside of the splint."

Griffin is eligible to return from the injured list on Sept. 4, which would put him on track to help this club over the final few weeks. If the Pirates can stay in the playoff race, Griffin's return could help propel them forward.

Griffin has been taking things day-by-day, allowing the injury to heal in the best way it can. But it's been a frustrating experience for the young star, especially with the team trying to get into the postseason.

"It's tough just because we're in the thick of it. We're fighting hard, and I can't really help," Griffin said. "Just have to sit back and watch. But I believe everything happens for a reason, so I'm just trying to stay as ready as I can. So whenever I'm cleared to go, I can get back as fast as I can."

Griffin has been a breath of fresh air for this Pirates team, with him showcasing all his talent before the injury. The 20-year-old has played in 59 games this season, hitting .276 with five home runs and 25 runs batted in, while putting up an OPS of .736.

His discipline at the plate, especially as a rookie, has been impressive, and is why the Pirates are so high on his future. Griffin has looked like a future superstar, so losing him for any stretch of time has hurt this team.

The additions at the trade deadline should only help Pittsburgh down the stretch. But getting Griffin back will be the biggest boost for this club, and maybe the postseason could be in their sights.

title: One Vikings offensive playmaker is on his way to the Hall of Fame

fullText:
For any player who puts on pads and a helmet, the idea of being a pro football player. From there, if that dream is achieved, the idea could then lead to talk of a second contract and more to lead a complete football life. For a very few, special players, there is the rainbow at the end that leads to the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

This weekend, the latest class will be heading to Canton to be enshrined, led by two NFC South legends, Luke Kuechly and Drew Brees. But with all the celebrations centered around that, some folks have started to wonder who else could become a Hall of Famer.

CBS Sports' Bryan DeArdo went through every NFL team and made some decisions on players who could be enshrined eventually. For the Vikings, he mentioned Justin Jefferson isn't a Hall of Famer but "is on his way."

He writes, "Jefferson is off to a torrid start. Despite missing time with an injury in 2023, Jefferson still went over 1,000 yards while recording the most yards in NFL history for a player's first five seasons after amassing 1,533 yards in 2024. It'll be interesting to see how he gels with Kyler Murray if Murray wins the starting job over J.J. McCarthy. Jefferson will go over 9,000 receiving yards and 50 touchdowns by the end of this season, most likely."

Jefferson has a chance to really be remembered as one of this generation's best wide receivers. He has overcome poor quarterback play, thrives with good play, and has the attitude and physical traits to be enshrined in Canton eventually.

title: Diamondbacks vs. Dodgers updates. Carroll's tough luck, AJ Puk done
description: The Arizona Diamondbacks open a three-game series against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Friday, Aug. 7, at Chase Field. Follow our live updates.
fullText:
The ball left Corbin Carroll's bat at 110 mph and was headed toward the right-center field gap before San Diego Padres center fielder Jackson Merrill made a sliding grab. The play from the first inning on Thursday night, Aug. 6, was the sort of tough-luck moment that sums up how Carroll has been feeling at the plate in recent weeks.

For the better part of a month, the Diamondbacks have been playing as well as any team in baseball. Somehow, they have been doing it without much in the way of offensive contributions from Carroll or Ketel Marte, their top two hitters.

For his part, Carroll says he still has "a long way to go" to feel the way he wants against right-handed pitchers, but he doesn't think the numbers he has been putting up lately — he is hitting just .211 since the All-Star break — accurately reflect how he has been feeling.

"I think if you look at the expected numbers since the break they've been pretty good," Carroll said. "I think we talked earlier in the year and I felt like the batted-ball luck had kind of gone my way. I kind of feel the opposite of that right now. I feel like a lot of balls I'm putting in play are finding a man out there. I'm trying not to get too caught up in that and go out there and keep playing and not press for results."

Carroll is right about his expected numbers. Since the break, his expected average (.248) and slug (.469) are better than his actual average (.211) and slug (.469).

He said he has been working in the batting cage using balls that generate "extra ride," which has helped him keep from getting under balls and popping them up.

"Just hitting a few more balls on a line," he said. "That's probably been the biggest thing, I would say. Just a little less extreme with the ball flight, a few more line drives."

Other than that, he credits a couple of days off after the All-Star Game with helping him deal with some "nagging" injuries.

"The little stuff adds up," he said. "I haven't had any off days. Only off days I've taken have been because I've not been able to go. I think having a couple of days over the break, that Wednesday and Thursday, has helped."

The Diamondbacks will no longer have the services of left-handed reliever A.J. Puk this season, manager Torey Lovullo announced prior to the team's game against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Friday, Aug. 7.

Puk has been shut down about two months after the onset of left shoulder discomfort during a rehab outing with Triple-A Reno in June. He had already been trying to come back from left elbow surgery last year.

"He will just rest and recover through the rest of this year, through the offseason and get ready for a very healthy '27," Lovullo said.

"He worked as hard as he possibly could, it just didn't work out for him this year."

Right-handed pitcher Zac Gallen (elbow inflammation) met with Lovullo after recent imaging and threw a 25-pitch bullpen on Aug. 7. He reported feeling good.

Right-hander Corbin Burnes (right shoulder strain) also threw a 25-pitch bullpen session.

Outfielder Lourdes Gurriel Jr. (right adductor strain) needs his recent imaging evaluated after an injury setback, but Lovullo said he is "still on a very good path."

Right-handed pitcher Ryne Nelson (strained right elbow) is feeling good after throwing off flat ground on Aug. 7. Reliever Ryan Thompson (strained back) will start his progression on Aug. 10 and outfielder Tommy Troy will take live batting practice on Aug. 8 to test out his injured shoulder.

Right-hander Drey Jameson (hip injury) will throw in a facility game at Salt River Fields. Outfielder Jordan Lawlar (hamstring) will play in his third Double-A game on Friday and is set to play on Aug. 8, with the possibility of moving on to play rehab games at Triple-A Reno.

"We're getting very close with him," Lovullo said of Lawlar. "He's missed here. He's going to help this team win baseball games. And when he comes back, we need him at 100 percent where he can play the same type of back-to-back games."

Right-handed pitcher Justin Martinez (elbow surgery recovery) was scheduled to pitch for Class A Visalia in a rehab outing in Fresno, and right-handed pitcher Michael Soroka is getting close to a return after throwing a bullpen session at Chase Field on Aug. 7.

Lefty Blake Walston is pitching in games after long-term rehab from left elbow surgery and is set to throw two innings and 35 pitches in Reno.

The Diamondbacks recalled right-handed reliever Kade Strowd from Triple-A Reno on Friday, Aug. 7, after they optioned lefty Kohl Drake to Reno following his 3⅔-inning effort on Thursday, Aug. 6 in a loss to San Diego.

"Kohl unfortunately hit some bumps in the road," Lovullo said. "We needed the extra reliever. We tapped into it a little bit (Thursday) with our length guy (three innings from Philip Abner). Strowd coming up here has been throwing the ball real good in Triple-A. He's able to give us multiple innings."

Diamondbacks 3B Nolan Arenado was announced as the Diamondbacks' Heart and Hustle Award winner for the 2026 season, an honor handed out by the Major League Baseball Players Association.

The award is annually given to active players who exemplify a true passion for the game and who best embody the spirit, values and traditions of the game of baseball.

Arenado, in his 13th MLB season, will be presented the award prior to the Diamondbacks-Dodgers game on Saturday, Aug. 8.

Former Diamondbacks Paul Goldschmidt (Yankees) and Jake McCarthy (Rockies) were the honorees for their respective teams.

Diamondbacks RHP Merrill Kelly (8-9, 5.04) vs. Dodgers RHP Roki Sasaki (5-5, 4.64).

At Chase Field: Kelly had been on a good roll until he gave up five earned runs at Cleveland on Sunday, Aug. 2. In that game, he had five strikeouts, four walks and ran his streak to 16 games pitching at least five innings. No team has given Kelly fits like the Dodgers. Kelly is 0-11 in 17 career starts against L.A., with 16 home runs given up in his career. ... Sasaki has won his past two starts and has clearly improved as a starting pitcher over last season. His numbers aren't out-of-this-world great, but the 24-year-old from Japan has made 19 starts after an injury-filled 2025. Opponents have 20 home runs off Sasaki in his 99 innings of work in 2026. He'll make his second career start and third appearance against the Diamondbacks.

Saturday, Aug. 8: At Chase Field, 5:10 p.m., Diamondbacks RHP Brandon Pfaadt (6-1, 3.66) vs. Dodgers RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (11-7, 2.76).

Sunday, Aug. 9: At Chase Field, 1:10 p.m., Diamondbacks LHP Eduardo Rodriguez (10-4, 2.71) vs. Dodgers LHP Justin Wrobleski (11-3, 3.31).

Monday, Aug. 10: At Chase Field, 6:40 p.m., Diamondbacks RHP Michael Soroka (8-3, 3.07) vs. Rockies RHP Gabriel Hughes (0-3, 4.25).

title: NFL Personality Rips ‘Soft as Brie Cheese’ Packers in NFC North Verdict
description: The Green Bay Packers are trying to move past a collapse that ended a promising 2025 season.Colin Cowherd already sees a problem that could follow them into 2026.Cowherd took aim at head coach Matt LaFleur and Green Bay’s toughness during the Aug. 7 edition of “The Herd,” questioning whether the Packers have enough edge to […] The post NFL Personality Rips ‘Soft as Brie Cheese’ Packers in NFC North Verdict appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The Green Bay Packers are trying to move past a collapse that ended a promising 2025 season.

Colin Cowherd already sees a problem that could follow them into 2026.

Cowherd took aim at head coach Matt LaFleur and Green Bay's toughness during the Aug. 7 edition of "The Herd," questioning whether the Packers have enough edge to survive a loaded NFC North.

"Soft as brie cheese in a town that loves aged cheddar," via The Herd's segment shared on X.

The post added that Cowherd believes LaFleur and the Packers "aren't tough enough to win big" in the division.

"Soft as brie cheese in a town that loves aged cheddar."@colincowherd argues Matt LaFleur & the Packers aren't tough enough to win big in the stacked NFC North pic.twitter.com/StvkwsH4np

— Herd w/Colin Cowherd (@TheHerd) August 7, 2026

It's pointed reproval for a coach who has won plenty of regular-season games in Green Bay.

LaFleur enters his eighth season with a 76-40-1 record, six playoff appearances and a new multiyear contract.

The question surrounding him has gone toward the up-in-the-air direction.

The Packers know LaFleur can get them into January. But Cowherd and others question whether his teams have the edge to finish once they get there.

GettyGREEN BAY, WISCONSIN – DECEMBER 07: Head coach Matt Lafleur of the Green Bay Packers reacts to a unsportsmanlike conduct penalty during the second quarter against the Chicago Bears at Lambeau Field on December 07, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images)

Green Bay gave Cowherd plenty of material during the final weeks of 2025.

The Packers were 9-3-1 before losing their final four regular-season games. Their season ended with a 31-27 wild-card loss to the Chicago Bears after Green Bay led 21-3 at halftime and 27-16 in the fourth quarter.

Jordan Love threw for 323 yards and four touchdowns in the loss, but the offense went through four third-quarter possessions while picking up only one first down.

The late-game problems went past one night.

NFL.com noted when LaFleur signed his extension that the Packers became the first team since the 1970 merger to lose three games in one season, including the playoffs, after holding a lead of at least 10 points in the final five minutes.

Two of those losses came against Chicago.

Injuries deserve a place in the discussion.

Micah Parsons suffered a torn ACL in Week 15, and Green Bay dealt with other significant absences down the stretch.

Still, the way games slipped away can't out of view.

Packers president Ed Policy did not see it as a reason to move on from LaFleur. Green Bay signed LaFleur, general manager Brian Gutekunst and executive vice president/director of football operations Russ Ball to multiyear extensions in January.

GettyLOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA – FEBRUARY 09: Colin Cowherd attends the The Volume Anniversary Party on February 09, 2022 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Jerod Harris/Getty Images for The Volume )

Cowherd's denunciation also has history behind it.

He made a similar argument in November 2022, saying the Packers had become "softer" under LaFleur and questioning the team's identity after a loss to Philadelphia.

Up to today, the quarterback has changed and much of the roster has turned over.

But Cowherd is harping on the same issue.

There is also a difference between LaFleur being under pressure and being on the hot seat.

Green Bay gave him a legitimate multiyear commitment less than seven months ago.

Policy said in March that it had "never been clearer" to him that the Packers had the right football leadership in place. He also said he had decided before the playoff game that he wanted LaFleur back.

That puts the focus on what happens on the field.

LaFleur has a 3-6 playoff record, and Green Bay has failed to reach the NFC Championship Game since the 2020 season.

The Packers have also gone one-and-done in each of the past two postseasons.

Cowherd's cheese line will get the attention, but the actual challenge sits underneath it.

Green Bay has already committed to LaFleur.

At any rate, his team has to show it can close the games that have kept it from becoming a championship team.

fullText:
NEW YORK — It sounds like Carlos Rodón will rejoin the Yankees' rotation soon.

The southpaw, out with elbow inflammation since June 30, is scheduled to make his first rehab start at Triple-A on Saturday. The plan is for Rodón to throw close to 50 pitches for the RailRiders.

From there, Rodón may or may not make one more rehab start, manager Aaron Boone said Friday. Either way, the Yankees will activate the pitcher before he's fully built up and "definitely probably piggyback him" in his initial starts, Boone said.

With a number of off days on the upcoming schedule and five healthy starters already in their rotation, the Yankees should be able to make that strategy work without taxing their bullpen. The long-held assumption has been that the Bombers will move Ryan Weathers or Will Warren to the pen anyway once Rodón returns, so either could be the piggyback pitcher while staying stretched out in this scenario.

Rodón, 33, went 4-2 with a 3.30 ERA over nine starts before going back on the IL.

He initially hoped to miss minimal time due to the inflammation, but he's been out over a month now. He said that multiple rounds of shots — he's gotten PRP and orthovisc injections — are to blame for the prolonged timeline.

"I always try to get back as quick as I can," Rodón said Friday. "I feel like anybody in this situation would. I wouldn't say anything delayed me. We just had a plan with the injections, and when you're scheduling injections and trying to throw in between them, it kind of makes it harder to figure out when you can throw, when you can't. Because when you get an injection, you might need a day off. Obviously, you take the first day off. You might need a couple more days.

So obviously, I would love to be pitching for our team right now. But right now, it's just building pitch count and getting in games, and that's it."

title: Denver Summit-Utah Royals match pushed back 6 hours due to extreme heat as NWSL weather policy receives scrutiny
description: Temperatures are set to approach 100 degrees in Denver on Saturday, with wildfire smoke and the city's altitude adding to a potentially risky playing environment.
fullText:
A matchup between the Denver Summit and Utah Royals has been significantly postponed due to extreme heat and other environmental factors, the NWSL announced Friday.

The match, which was set to kick off at 2 p.m. MT on Saturday in Denver, has been rescheduled to 8 p.m.

The NWSL said the decision to push back the match was made after consulting with climate experts, doctors from both teams and the NWSL Players' Association.

"The healthy and safety of our players, staff, officials and fans remains our top priority and will continue to guide our decision-making in this matter," the league wrote in a statement.

Saturday's match will be held at Centennial Stadium, the Summit's temporary venue while the team builds a new stadium in Denver. Centennial, Colorado, where the stadium is located, is just southeast of Denver.

An update from the NWSL on tomorrow’s match between Denver Summit FC and Utah Royals FC. pic.twitter.com/cUButIw5Ll

Temperatures are set to near 100 degrees in Denver on Saturday. In addition, the area will be affected by air-quality issues stemming from wildfires in the western part of the country. Both of those issues will be exacerbated by the altitude, an ever-present issue in Denver, which sits one mile above sea level.

That combination, per the league, led to "unique medical considerations that warranted additional precaution beyond the operational standards established in the league's Gameday Heat Safety Policy." The league's policy, which uses the wet bulb globe temperature to measure safety risk, is usually used to factor humidity and cloud cover into the baseline heat.

The NWSL's weather policy has been criticized over the past few years, especially as weather conditions worsen due to climate change. Last August, a game between the Kansas City Current and Orlando Pride was delayed more than three hours due to excess heat.

The Athletic reported after that game that NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman had threatened to fine the Current over a disagreement about whether it was safe to play, with Berman citing the potentially high cost of missing the game's broadcast window.

With the league's heat policy facing scrutiny (and Berman's alleged threat receiving backlash) after that game, the NWSL updated its weather policy ahead of the 2026 season, adding additional hydration breaks during games within a set wet bulb globe temperature range.

More changes are likely coming this offseason. A summer marred by wildfire smoke across the country has raised concerns about additional weather issues that can affect games.

In the Queens Classic last month, when Gotham FC beat the Washington Spirit at Citi Field, the game proceeded as scheduled despite an air quality index of 170 — just below the NWSL's threshold for postponing the match. Players after the game said the air quality was less than ideal for playing, even with two hydration breaks per half to try to combat the effects of the smoke.

During a midseason news conference Wednesday, Berman said the league would be reassessing policies at the end of the season and acknowledged that the Gotham-Spirit game would be used as a "data point" in that analysis.

title: Misdemeanor gun charges against James Harden dropped
description: Harden had been arrested in Houston in June when police found a gun in his car.
fullText:
At the request of the Harris County district attorney's office in Houston, a misdemeanor gun charge against Cleveland Cavaliers guard James Harden has been dismissed after he completed an alternative resolution program, reports the Associated Press.

Alternative programs are a fairly common way for people to avoid a criminal record for a minor offense. In this case, Harden likely did some community service in the Houston area, although the agreement did not detail exactly what he did, according to the AP.

Harden, an 11-time All-Star, had been arrested on June 13 for having a gun in the cupholder of his car. He had been driving a car as part of a multi-car group when one of the other drivers was pulled over, according to the Harris County police report. Harden had pulled up behind the police and the other vehicle, and while interacting with the police, one officer noticed Harden had a gun in the cupholder of his car, according to the report. Harden allegedly confirmed the gun was his, which led to his arrest and booking.

Harden played eight seasons — his peak seasons, statistically — in Houston and has close ties to the city. He spends much of his offseason there every year.

Harden, 36, technically still remains a free agent, but is expected to re-sign with the Cavaliers in the coming weeks. He opted out of the $42.3 million he was owed to give the Cavaliers more cap space to chase LeBron James (they struck out there) or make other moves. He is expected to re-sign in Cleveland for around $30 million a season (depending on what other moves the team makes) for multiple years. Harden was traded from the LA Clippers to Cleveland in the middle of this past season, and between the two teams he averaged 23.6 points and 8 assists per game while shooting 37.5% from 3-point range.

title: Brooks Koepka has a new putter (again), and Jason Day's bag overhaul | Tour Report
description: In this week's Tour Report, Brooks Koepka has a new putter for the fourth time this season, and Jason Day makes major changes.
fullText:
Welcome to Fully Equipped's weekly Tour equipment report. Every Friday of PGA Tour weeks (plus other times, if news warrants), GOLF equipment editor Jack Hirsh runs you through some of the biggest news surrounding golf clubs on Tour, including changes, tweaks and launches.

When you say the word "Teryllium," it has a special meaning to Scotty Cameron fans. We're going to assume that includes Brooks Koepka.

Teryllium is a unique-to-Cameron alloy made from a combination of copper and 11 other metals that for the last 30 years has given its putters an unmistakable soft, yet responsive, feel. The material first came to prominence when Tiger Woods used a Newport Tel3 to win the Masters by 12 in 1997.

More recently, Teryllium has shown up in a number of Scotty Cameron special releases and Tour putters, including several made specifically for Koepka, who won all five of his major championships using Teryllium Newport 2s.

This week, at the Wyndham Championship, Koepka is back in a putter with the iconic copper insert. This time, it's a new Phantom 3.2 mallet.

Koepka has been on a putter search this season. He lost nearly two-and-a-half strokes a round in his first start back on the PGA Tour at the Farmers Insurance Open and immediately switched from his Scotty Cameron T22 Newport 2 gamer to a TaylorMade Spider Tour X.

The Spider Tour X lasted until Myrtle Beach when he broke the putter in apparent frustration. The following week at the PGA Championship, Koepka tried a then-recently launched Spider Tour V with long plumber's neck but still lost strokes on the greens for the sixth time in eight starts.

Putter change for Brooks Koepka as he makes his final push for the playoffs. 

Koepka has a new Scotty Cameron Phantom 3.2 with a custom Teryllium insert. This really isn't surprising given that Koepka used a Newport 2 putters with the soft copper-colored insert to win all five… pic.twitter.com/0U63KUxpD4

He used a third putter in as many weeks at the CJ Cup Byron Nelson, when he went back to Scotty Cameron, this time a Studio Style Fastback 1.5 mid mallet. Like his Teryllium putters, the Studio Style also has a soft-feeling insert, but it's made from Studio Carbon Steel and sports the company's chain-link mill pattern.

The Fastback sparked his best round of the season, a 63, in the opening round in Dallas while recording his second-best SG: Putting round of the year.

But since then, Koepka has been held back by injury and finished only one other event, the Open Championship, where he logged a T28. He lost more than a stroke on the greens at Royal Birkdale. Still, his SG: Putting on Tour ranking of 116th this season has improved from 141 since switching to Fastback 1.5. Meanwhile, he ranks 8th in SG: Approach.

Apparently, that's led Koepka to go back to the familiar feel of the Teryllium insert this week in a new package, the Phantom 3.2.

Scotty Cameron 2026 Phantom 3.2 Custom Putter

ALSO AVAILABLE AT: PGA TOUR Superstore, Titleist

This actually isn't the first week Koepka has tested Teryllium again this season. At the PGA Championship, he tried out a custom Phantom 9.5R, the same shape used by Cameron Young and Justin Thomas, with a Teryllium insert, but decided the putter was too heavy.

With nearly all of Cameron's current models sporting an insert, the Cameron Tour team has done some cool experiments with different insert materials including Teryllium, Studio Stainless Steel (SSS) and aluminum.

The Phantom 3.2 is the newest shape in the Phantom mallet family and is designed specifically to have a more forward CG and play similarly to a blade. The ".2" plumber's neck is also the same hosel Koepka had on his previous Newport 2s.

In his opening-round 67 at Sedgefield, Koepka gained nearly 2.6 strokes on the greens, 9th in the field. But he has work to do as he needs at least a solo fourth finish this week to qualify for next week's FedEx Cup Playoffs and he started the second round six off the lead.

Jason Day has made nearly a complete bag overhaul this week. 

Out with his Avoda irons and wedges and in with Callaway's new Apex MB '26 and X Forged 5-iron.

He swapped his red Spider Tour for a new custom Odyssey White Hot OG No. 5. pic.twitter.com/h2nl0LPT65

It appears Jason Day is done with his testing of Avoda's curved face irons.

The former World No. 1 had been playing prototype sets of the company's irons and wedges with unique bulge-and-roll characteristics similar to the ones Bryson DeChambeau played since last fall, but he's making a change this week as he ranks outside the top 150 in SG: Approach.

Instead, Day has picked up a set of Callaway's new 2026 Apex MB irons and Opus SP wedges. But that's not all he's changing. He also added two Callaway Quantum fairway woods (a Quantum Ti 3-wood and TD 5-wood) along with a custom all black Odyssey White Hot OG No. 5.

Day made TaylorMade's red Spider Tour famous by earning the world's top ranking and winning the 2015 PGA Championship with it, but he told GolfWRX he used Odyssey's No. 5 as a junior.

All the new clubs retain the KBS TG Black and TGI shafts he was playing previously. The only clubs he's keeping in the bag are his Ping G430 LST driver and TaylorMade Stealth 2 7-wood.

That means he's still playing the same 3w-5w-7w setup he's used for most of the year before he drops to his next longest club, a new X Forged JDM 5-iron.

title: Blake Snell to return from IL on Tuesday as Dodgers rotation begins to take shape

fullText:
The Los Angeles Dodgers might be on a losing streak, but they're about to get a rather important player back from the injured list.

Dodgers manager Dave Roberts told reporters Friday that Blake Snell will return to the rotation on Tuesday against the Kansas City Royals, according to The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya. Also, trade deadline pickup Tarik Skubal will reportedly make his Dodger Stadium debut on Monday.

Snell has made only one start all season, having begun 2026 on the injured list due to shoulder fatigue. He made that single (bad) start in May before returning to the IL, this time due to loose bodies in his pitching elbow. He wound up undergoing the same procedure to remove them as Skubal did weeks earlier.

While Skubal needed only 38 days to return from his loose bodies, Snell took a longer road back. The two-time Cy Young Award winner began a rehab assignment on July 18 and has made four starts since then, topping out at 73 pitches on Tuesday for the Triple-A Oklahoma City Comets.

This would hardly be the first season in which Snell has no-showed the first half, only to look like one of the best arms in the game in the second half. He holds a 4.00 career ERA in the first half and a 2.33 ERA in the second half, with nearly equal innings despite the first half of the MLB season taking up more of the calendar.

Snell was a key pitcher for the Dodgers during their World Series run last year, posting a 3.18 ERA across six appearances (five starts, plus a relief appearance in their Game 7 win).

The Dodgers will happily welcome him back as their rotation starts to take form. The team has plugged along with the likes of Eric Lauer and Emmet Sheehan, who was optioned earlier this week, in its rotation, but L.A.'s postseason rotation is almost certain to feature Snell, Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and one of Shohei Ohtani or Tyler Glasnow.

Glasnow is also currently on the IL due to lower-back spasms and recently began a rehab assignment.

Ohtani has been off the mound since the first half due to knee discomfort.

OLTEWAH, Tenn. – For Rachel Heck, Thursday's 1-up victory over Anna Davis at the 2026 U.S. Women's Amateur was about more than advancing to the next round.

This week marks Heck's third competitive event of the year, but it wasn't until her match against Davis, the 2022 Augusta National Women's Amateur champion — which came down to the final hole — that she felt something she'd been missing for a long time.

"So much excitement," Heck said after winning her match, "It was so fun to feel those emotions again, the adrenaline and the nerves. I haven't felt that in a long time."

The win marked Heck's first match-play victory at the U.S. Women's Amateur since her quarterfinal run in 2023, a meaningful milestone as she makes her return to competitive golf.

A former NCAA individual champion and two-time Curtis Cup competitor, Heck showed flickers of the form that made her one of the game's most recognizable amateurs, answering every challenge from Davis before closing out the match on the 18th green.

But it wasn't just the thought of winning that had Heck experiencing a familiar wave of emotions. It was also the intensity and pressure that comes with battling out a close match, and it wasn't until she was in the heat of battle that she realized it was the very thing she had been lacking.

"This is the feeling I really wanted when I decided to get back into amateur golf and play some more," she said. "I wanted the opportunity to come down the stretch in a match and have my heart racing."

fullText:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are adding two of their best starters, Blake Snell and Tarik Skubal, are bringing serious star power to Dodger Stadium.

Finally, after months of rehab and recovery, Snell is pitching for the Dodgers again, this time for the major league club.

He will take the mound on Tuesday against the Kansas City Royals, a team with a lackluster offense that will set up Snell for a smooth start.

Skubal takes the ball on Monday, right before Snell, making his full-fledged debut at Dodger Stadium.

The Dodgers need quality pitching badly; with Skubal putting up one of the only good starts over the last few weeks for LA, he will be tasked with once again keeping the team in the game.

Snell, on the other hand, has the task of sharpening up his pitching for the postseason, all while staying healthy and providing quality innings to a pitching staff rocked with new players entering and exiting the active roster.

LA is riding a six-game losing streak, dropping eight of their last 10 games, mainly due to the bullpen and rotation struggling.

Snell will likely end up taking Eric Lauer's spot in the rotation, and from the outset, the Dodgers will likely only push him around 80 pitches before asking more from him as time goes on.

Lauer, for the most part, has been good at preventing runs and putting the Dodgers in spot where they can win, as a former Cy Young award winner, the expectations for Snell will be higher.

Snell has made it clear that his arm feels better than ever after his elbow surgery. He posted a 2.35 ERA and a 2.69 FIP last year in 11 starts

His stuff, at his best, is elite and when he can command his pitches, hitters have a tough time dealing with him.

It is quite exciting to think that the best from Snell is yet to come, though next week will be the first inkling into whether or not that is the case.

title: What counts as cooking? In defense of the store-bought sauce
description: “I didn’t cook dinner last night,” my sister mentioned to me the other week. She has a one-year-old and a three-year-old, a combination of ages that practically guarantees a baseline level of perpetual exhaustion. “Oh!” I replied. “Wait.
fullText:
“I didn’t cook dinner last night,” my sister mentioned to me the other week.

She has a one-year-old and a three-year-old, a combination of ages that practically guarantees a
baseline level of perpetual exhaustion.

“Oh!” I replied. “Wait.” I tried to rationalize what that meant. My sister sounded too blasé to
imply that they had all simply given up and gone hungry (and if that was indeed the case, it was
an odd way to bring it up). “So… you ordered Uber Eats?”

“No, I made toast with scrambled eggs.”

This didn’t make any sense to me. “But that is cooking! You cooked!”

“I guess,” she countered. “But not from scratch — it wasn’t cooking. I didn’t cook like you cook.”

I have been thinking about this conversation for a while now. Why didn’t this count as cooking?

At some point society collectively decided (when I wasn’t paying attention) that cooking only really
counts if it involves chopping up aromatics, blooming spices, and dirtying half the pots in the
kitchen. If it comes together in under ten minutes, relies on a store-bought shortcut, or doesn’t
match the idealised family dinner, we demote it. We didn’t cook, we merely assembled.

But anything you make to feed yourself or your family is cooking. It doesn’t need to be fancy, and
it certainly doesn’t need to be from scratch.

My sister, my mum, and I have always been massive fans of MasterChef Australia. During the years
we all lived at home, we would organize our nights around MasterChef, arguing about what we would
do with the mystery box ingredients, shouting at the contestants during the team challenges1, and in awe of the
complexity of the pressure tests.

It is phenomenal television, but watching it for almost twenty years can subtly recalibrate your
perception of what a Tuesday night dinner should entail. When you spend an hour every evening2, watching amateur home cooks frantically trying to
execute a flawless ballotine of chicken, complete with a perfectly clarified consommé, micro-herb
garnishes, and a savory tuile before the clock runs out, your internal benchmark for cooking
quietly shifts3.

When the show first premiered in 2009, it fundamentally
changed the country’s food culture,
triggering what the media dubbed the “MasterChef effect”. Whenever a previously niche ingredient or
specific cut of meat — like pork belly, beef cheeks, or pomegranate molasses — was featured on an
episode, major supermarkets would famously sell out of it the very next day.
The franchise elevated the everyday vernacular of the Australian home cook, injecting
restaurant-industry terms like “plating up,” “sous-vide,” and “hero-ing an ingredient” into
suburban kitchens. Australian cafe menus were permanently altered, with favourites like eggs on
toast and smashed avocado making way for unique fusion creations such as slow cooked beef brisket
rendang benedict, with curry leaf hollandaise (and, inevitably, dollops of fresh coriander oil,
because nothing says breakfast like an herb extraction).

While it was a brilliant, much-needed celebration of Australia’s diverse, multicultural food scene, it
also accidentally cemented a new, intimidating standard. It created an illusion that amateur
cooking was no longer just about sustenance; it was about executing professional-grade gastronomy.

You can actually see this shift if you revisit past MasterChef seasons. The food in the early
years was decidedly simpler. The season one finale famously finished with a whole chicken
challenge: Julie Goodwin made a Sunday roast, and Poh Ling Yeoh made Hainanese chicken rice. This
escalation didn’t go unnoticed in our house — mum would frequently annoy my sister and me in later
seasons by despairing at the lack of actual home cooks. “These are not home cooks!” she would
mutter darkly at the screen. “I bet they have secret restaurant experience.”4

Add to this the modern aesthetic of the Instagram and TikTok kitchen — gorgeous, cinematic reels of
people fermenting their own hot sauce, folding laminated pastry dough, or making insanely intricate packed lunches for their kids —
and the kitchen is no longer a place of domestic utility, but a stage. A place of competitive sport and lifestyle aesthetics.

When you are saturated in this media, you begin to compare your chaotic, weeknight survival tactics
to someone else’s performative hobby. If you aren’t making the pasta or tortillas by hand5, the inner critic whispers, you aren’t really cooking.

It wasn’t always this way. For most of human history, cooking was an inescapable daily chore,
primarily shouldered by women.

When the post-war convenience food boom hit in the 1950s and 60s, it promised a revolution. Products
like jarred sauces, canned soups, and boxed cake mixes were explicitly marketed as liberators. They
bought precious hours back from the stove, while making new techniques and cuisines accessible
(store-bought gelatin crystals, for example, provided an easy pathway to impressive jellies that
previously required grueling manual labor to extract).

But there was a catch — while some of these innovations were embraced wholeheartedly, home cooks felt guilty when using shortcuts that displaced the familiar,
nostalgic recipes they had grown up with, like relying on a packet of instant gravy. For centuries,
a mother’s worth had been tied directly to the stove; simply opening a cardboard box felt like a
dereliction of duty6.

You might assume that as these convenience foods became cheap, ubiquitous, and the unquestioned
backbone of the modern pantry, the stigma would have eventually worn off. But humans are remarkably
efficient at manufacturing new and exciting forms of guilt. I suspect the stigma never really
vanished; it just evolved.

Perhaps, as food delivery exploded and shortcuts became available to everyone, and social media and
reality TV became parts of daily life, cooking from scratch ceased to be a grim necessity and
morphed into something else: a status symbol. It seems to now signal that you possess the ultimate
modern luxury — free time. The guilt surrounding convenience foods simply evolved: what used to
be a dereliction of duty (the avoidance of hard labor) has morphed into a dereliction of status
(the feeling that you aren’t really ‘cooking’ at all).

It is entirely possible that we never actually stopped viewing the jar of pasta sauce as a culinary
failure; we just changed our reasoning for why it was a failure.

Whenever I catch myself slipping into this kind of culinary elitism, I think about my favourite
lasagna of all time: my mum’s.

Over the years, I have tried making lasagna from scratch more times than I can count. I have put a
frankly embarrassing amount of effort into it: braising beef short ribs for hours (once even
overnight!) to make a homemade ragù, whisking my arm numb making béchamel, sourcing artisanal
cheeses, and hand-cranking delicate sheets of fresh egg pasta.

These lasagnas were technically impressive, and they were delicious. But they always fell slightly
short — they were not the lasagna I craved.

The lasagna I am nostalgic for is the one my mum made. She did not braise short ribs. She did not
knead pasta dough. Her lasagna was constructed in about an hour on a busy weeknight. She used
supermarket beef mince, a jar of Dolmio bolognese sauce, a jar of Dolmio béchamel sauce7, and
handfuls of pre-grated cheddar cheese straight from the bag, simply because that was what she
always had on hand in the fridge.

Was it traditional? No. Was it from scratch? Definitely not.

But it was bubbling, golden, and deeply comforting. When I eat lasagna today, that specific mix of
jarred bolognese sauce and melted cheddar is the exact flavour profile my heart is searching for.
My mum didn’t apologize for using Dolmio, or even consider that that wasn’t the ‘proper’ way to
make lasagna. She put a hot, delicious meal on the table.

The problem with viewing cooking strictly as ‘making things from scratch’ is that it completely
divorces the food from its actual purpose: nourishment (otherwise known as, keeping people alive
and reasonably happy).

When my sister stood in her kitchen, undoubtedly exhausted after wrangling a toddler and a baby all
day, she still cracked eggs into a pan. She still tended to the heat. She buttered the toast. She
transformed those basic ingredients into a warm meal that sustained her family for another night.

That is the essence of cooking.

While there is nothing more I love than spending hours in the kitchen, exploring new techniques and,
yes, sometimes making complicated dishes ‘from scratch’, we need to give ourselves grace to embrace
the shortcuts. A jar of store-bought pasta sauce, a bag of pre-washed salad greens, a frozen pie
crust, or a simple plate of scrambled eggs on toast — these aren’t failures of culinary ambition.
They are just the practical realities of keeping ourselves fed.

The next time you throw together a meal using three ingredients and a microwave, or assemble a
dinner entirely out of things you found in the pantry, resist the urge to say, “I didn’t really
cook tonight.” You fed yourself. You fed your family.

I spoke to my sister a little while later, and she shared a funny update about that night.

After she plated the eggs and toast and sat down at the table, her three-year-old took a bite,
looked up, and said, “Mummy, I really love this. It is so yummy.”

It was incredibly cute, but it made her laugh — her husband is usually the one who takes on the more
involved, elaborate dinners in their household, and he almost never gets that kind of glowing,
unprompted praise (this later made me think, there is a distinct lack of Michelin stars awarded by
the under-five demographic).

It was a perfect reminder that the people we are cooking for aren’t grading our technique
like MasterChef judges, and they aren’t checking to see if we made the sauce from scratch. They
are just happy to be fed, and happy to be sitting at the table with us.

While a 15-minute audit is crucial for catching immediate issues, a robust backup strategy for your homelab, especially as a college student, needs to extend beyond reactive checks. Think proactively about what data is truly irreplaceable and what the academic cost would be if it vanished. This isn't just about your game server saves or media library; it's about your senior thesis, your machine learning project's training data, your research paper drafts, or the complex code for your capstone project. Losing these could mean redoing months of work, missing deadlines, or even impacting your graduation.

For students balancing studies with homelab tinkering, implementing a tiered backup approach is highly effective. Start by identifying your most critical academic data and segregating it. For instance, code repositories might go to a Git service (like GitHub or GitLab) *and* be backed up locally, while research papers could be synced to cloud storage (like OneDrive or Google Drive) *and* included in your regular homelab backups. This layering provides multiple recovery points, dramatically reducing the risk of total data loss.

Consider the "3-2-1 rule" adapted for your student budget and setup: at least three copies of your data, stored on two different types of media, with one copy off-site. For instance, your Proxmox VM backups might be on your NAS (media 1), a copy could be synced to an external hard drive you keep off-campus (media 2, off-site), and the critical files within those VMs could also be mirrored to a cloud service. This multi-pronged approach ensures that even if your entire homelab goes down due to a power surge, theft, or a critical hardware failure, your academic progress remains secure.

A manual 15-minute audit is a great starting point, but for true peace of mind and to reduce human error, you'll want to move towards automating as much of your backup verification as possible. This doesn't mean becoming a shell scripting guru overnight, but rather leveraging simple scripts to perform routine checks that go beyond merely confirming a backup job completed successfully. A "successful" log entry doesn't guarantee data integrity; a corrupted backup archive is still a successful file creation.

Start with basic integrity checks. For Proxmox, this might involve running vma_info on a backup archive or even scripting a small restore to a temporary location to ensure the VM boots. For Docker, verify that a restored container's data volume contains the expected files or that a specific service starts correctly. While a full restore of every backup might be impractical, a rotating verification schedule – where you randomly pick one critical VM or container backup each week to partially restore and test – can catch latent issues before they become critical.
