title: These NYC centers allow hard drug use in-house. Nearly 5 years in, is it helping?
description: An addiction-services nonprofit approved by the city focuses on harm reduction for hard drug users — to the chagrin of some in the neighborhood.
fullText:
In a back room behind a colorful facade in northern Manhattan, drug users are smoking crack while nearby cubicles stand ready for heroin users to wrap tourniquets around their arms and inject themselves with new, sterilized needles.

It's all part of a 5-year-old experiment sanctioned by the city of New York, but not by the federal government, which has long-standing anti-"crack house" laws criminalizing facilities that allow for drug use.

Supporters say the supervised drug-use sites reduce overdose deaths and street drug use, and serve as a model for the rest of the country. But critics say the centers are magnets for hard drug users and dealers, leaving the local community feeling less safe.

"It's scary for the kids walking into school in the morning, seeing people in that state," said an educator at a nearby school who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

New York City has two facilities like this, known as overdose prevention centers, or OPCs. By supervising the use of addictive, illegal drugs, proponents say the sites remove barriers to healthcare and can lead to people getting off drugs or transitioning to less risky behaviors.

In a recent interview with CBS News, OnPoint NYC Executive Director Sam Rivera said his team has intervened in more than 2,100 overdoses with no fatalities, and has more than 7,000 registered participants who have used the facility's services 250,000 times since it opened in 2021.

"250,000 times people used inside with us, not in the parks, not in the street, not in the playgrounds, not in bathrooms," said Rivera.

Rivera gave CBS News a tour of OnPoint's facility in East Harlem, a neighborhood where problems with drug use have persisted for decades.

In addition to the smoking room and injection cubicles, OnPoint offers services such as primary medical care, addiction medication, art therapy, sleep rooms and laundry, as well as perks like massage, acupuncture, aromatherapy and, soon, hair styling.

They are amenities that might seem more at home in an upscale wellness center than a place where people can inject heroin just a few steps from the massage tables. But Rivera said the wellness therapies serve a purpose.

"Those things are medicine. Those things are reducing drug use, introducing people into an environment that loves them," he told CBS News. "Many of our folks haven't experienced that."

In the massage room, an OnPoint participant-turned-part-time employee said, "I did the acupuncture, for the first time my back feels better. I didn't believe it but it really works."

Outside of OnPoint's walls, however, some residents say they're not happy about what it means for their neighborhood.

"You couldn't pay me to walk down that street anymore," said Syderia Asberry-Chresfield, co-founder of the Greater Harlem Coalition. "The dealers don't even have to look for clients. Drugs are being sold in front of everyone's faces. It's a slap in the face."

CBS News met Led Black, founder of the local media organization Uptown Collective, who lives a few blocks away from another OnPoint location in Washington Heights.

"I have three daughters. They're not little, but they're still young, they still shouldn't have to deal with this," he said. "You don't want the kids downtown to see it. Why is it OK for the kids up here to see it?"

In a campaign ad, New York state attorney general candidate Saritha Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor running as a Republican, singled out OnPoint as an example of bad policy.

"The problem here is these sites take people in, they give them deadly drugs, and then they turn them right back out on the street and into the subways. That's not a solution," Komatireddy told CBS News. "I think it's unethical. I think it's cruel, and it's definitely illegal." (OnPoint has a space for users to stay indoors and be monitored while they are under the influence of drugs.)

She notes that the East Harlem location is directly across the street from an early childhood development center and two blocks down from a school with students in kindergarten through grade 12.

Last year, Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, a New York Republican, publicly asked then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to shut down the facility, citing federal law prohibiting illegal drugs.

"They're enabling addiction instead of actually getting people the treatment they need to get off drugs," Malliotakis told CBS News. "They're also letting dealers know where their clients are."

In the 1970s, amid rising drug use in America, a movement began that would evolve into what's known today as "harm reduction" policy, with a core principle of removing any judgment or coercion from drug treatment.

Providing clean needles and testing drugs for contaminants that can cause sudden death seemed like the humane way to address painful-to-kick addictions, keep people alive, and reduce infectious diseases.

Despite the compassion behind the policies, they were no match for the nation's growing addiction crisis or increasingly lethal drug supply in recent years. Federal data show the rate of drug overdose deaths quadrupled in the U.S. between 2002 and 2022, a problem largely driven by prescription opioid pills before ballooning into a full-blown opioid epidemic.

Overdose deaths climbed to a peak of almost 108,000 in 2022 before starting to decline, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Overdose prevention centers that supervise drug use in-house are an extension of the harm reduction approach. While still unfamiliar to most Americans, they've existed internationally for two decades, with one report finding more than 100 such facilities worldwide, including many across Europe.

The one in Vancouver, Canada, is probably the most well known and has been in operation since 2003. Vancouver saw a steady rise in overdose deaths until a peak in 2022.

Just two months after taking office, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani visited OnPoint to show support for the program.

"This weekend, the team at OnPoint NYC kept their doors open 24/7 so vulnerable New Yorkers had somewhere safe to go," Mamdani posted on X  in March, alongside photos of himself with Rivera and other staff.

OnPoint operates with about $19 million in annual funding from a mixture of city, state and private funds, including some opioid settlement money. The city of New York funds a lot of it through multi-year contracts worth about $17 million in total. However, city rules prohibit using any of those funds for the direct supervision of drug use, so the organization has to rely on other sources for that work.

OnPoint once had more than $2 million in grants from SAMHSA, the federal Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, which it lost after President Trump issued an executive order in July 2025 explicitly barring federal taxpayer dollars from funding "drug injection sites" or "illicit drug use."

Despite the belief among many city officials, public health practitioners and researchers studying the programs that overdose prevention facilities are effective and necessary, their future in America is far from certain.

Efforts to open similar facilities in Seattle, Portland, San Francisco and Chicago have all failed. (Those cities have other harm reduction programs, such as needle exchange programs and social services for drug users.) Only Rhode Island has been able to move forward providing supervised drug consumption since OnPoint opened in 2021.

Rivera said he still wants to expand and has a community of city officials who support the notion.

The NIH's National Institute on Drug Abuse writes that after 20 years of international experience, "it is unclear whether such facilities reduce overdose death rates overall."

Existing studies tend to show some reduced death rates near the facilities that become hard to detect in larger populations. One systematic study from 2021 of existing international research concluded that OPCs "may help reduce overdose morbidity" while another study of Canadian programs across British Columbia found "no evidence that they reduce local hospitalization or mortality rates."

New York City's experiment with supervised drug use has been running for nearly five years — enough to start drawing conclusions about its impact.

Over the past two years, overdose deaths citywide have been decreasing rapidly from the highest recorded year ever in 2023, which tracks with the national trend. The city's Department of Health did not name OnPoint directly, but in a press release touting harm-reduction programs, it credited the change to "several years of increased investment in evidence-based overdose prevention strategies in NYC."

The NIH is now funding a team of researchers to evaluate America's three supervised injection sites: the two OnPoint NYC facilities and a newer one in Providence, Rhode Island, called Project Weber/RENEW. The multi-year study is still ongoing, and while they have not drawn conclusions on mortality rates, one of the lead authors said in an interview with CBS News that he believes overdose prevention centers have had a positive effect on public health.

Charles Fain Lehman looks at the very same data and sees a net negative. He is a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute for Policy Research, a conservative think tank that has been a vocal critic of Mamdani's policies.

"There is a lot of evidence that interventions of this type generally do not have an appreciable effect on overdose deaths," Lehman told CBS News. "There's a fixed pool of resources available for helping people who are dealing with substance use disorder. If you're spending the dollars on an intervention that doesn't work, like supervised consumption sites … you're not spending dollars on [addiction medication] and evidence-based treatment."

A CBS News analysis of available crime data told two different stories between the two neighborhoods where OnPoint operates.

Felony crime complaints have risen steadily in the 34th Precinct, where the Washington Heights facility is located, since OnPoint opened in 2021. The precinct includes multiple city blocks, so the increase in felony crime complaints cannot be tied directly to OnPoint. Citywide complaints have also increased over most of that time, but more slowly than in the 34th.

In the 25th Precinct, where the East Harlem facility is located, felony complaints rose after 2019 and peaked in 2023. By 2025, felony complaints fell substantially but remained 10% above their pre-pandemic levels. The rest of the city fared worse, with felony complaints remaining near 2024 levels last year.

A CBS News review of 911 call data from the New York City Police Department showed most of the calls made from the OnPoint addresses were for ambulance services; relatively few calls required police response.

So far this year there have been 124 calls from the East Harlem location and 84 calls from the Washington Heights address.

A study in 2023 found no significant changes near the sites in "crime or disorder," which included 911 calls for trespass and 311 complaints.

Another study in the Journal for Experimental Criminology found a significant increase in property crimes near the Washington Heights location, where a Target store had recently opened. The study authors reasoned that placing the safe injection facility so near a location with easily shoplifted products created an environment ripe for theft. Notably, the study found no similar increase near the East Harlem facility and no increase in violent crimes in either location.

"This is our major conclusion, is that your location matters," said the study's co-author John Hall, a retired NYPD officer who is currently a PhD candidate at the Institute of Criminology at Cambridge University in England.

The NIH study's initial findings show that the sites seem to have a largely neutral effect on local business activity and drug-related criminal activity in their neighborhoods.

Brandon Marshall, one of the researchers on the NIH team evaluating America's overdose prevention centers, said, "OPCs can do many things. They can reduce public drug use, they can reduce 911 calls. They can help people access healthcare and treatment. They are not a panacea to all social problems in a neighborhood."

When the multi-year evaluation comes in from the NIH, it may move the debate about supervised drug consumption forward — or it may not.

Johns Hopkins bioethicist Travis Rieder argues that support for places like OnPoint will never be decided solely by the empirical data.

"I don't actually think it's why anyone believes what they believe," he said. "They have a view about what we should actually be helping people to do or not do, and then they find the evidence that best supports their view."

Rieder said he knows where he stands. "Here's what an overdose prevention site does: It says, 'You are welcome here, and I will watch over you so that you don't die today, and you're worth that. You deserve that because you're a human being and you have dignity.' And I think that's a really beautiful thing."

Black, the community activist, says he wants the researchers at universities studying OnPoint to spend a day in his shoes.

"Why should it be an addict-focused approach?" Black said. "I wish it were a community-focused approach."

–Jamie Korenblat and Max Moore contributed reporting.

title: Federal judge orders Virginia county to replace Confederate school names it restored in 2024
description: A federal judge has sided with the Virginia NAACP in its lawsuit against a county school board’s reinstatement of Confederate military names to two schools, saying the decision discriminated against B...
fullText:
ROANOKE, Va. (AP) — A federal judge has sided with the Virginia NAACP in its lawsuit against a county school board's reinstatement of Confederate military names to two schools, saying the decision discriminated against Black students and ordering the board to change the schools' monikers again.

In an opinion filed Thursday in U.S. District Court of Virginia, Judge Michael F. Urbanski said the school board in Shenandoah County violated Black students' rights under the 14th Amendment's equal protection clause, which forbids racial discrimination in state-supported institutions. The decision also violates the Equal Educational Opportunities Act, the court found.

Confederate army officers' names are "vestiges" of Shenandoah County's segregationist history that required separate schools for Black and white students.

"The Confederate names were restored with complete awareness of their historic legacy and ongoing discriminatory impact," Urbanski wrote. "In the court's view, the affirmative act of reinstating these vestiges of segregation is far more problematic than a passive failure to remove a long-standing name or symbol."

The judge ordered the board to settle on new school names "on a racially nondiscriminatory basis with all deliberate speed."

Unlike memorials named after Confederate figures, schools are places where children should have an "educational environment free of vestiges of racial discrimination," Urbanski added.

Jim Guynn, the attorney representing Shenandoah County, did not immediately respond to a phone message seeking comment.

In a statement Friday, the NAACP Virginia State Conference called the ruling "a decisive victory" for students.

"For decades, the practice of honoring Confederate leaders in Virginia schools has been steeped in a history of racial discrimination," said its president, the Rev. Cozy Bailey. "The school board's 2024 renaming decision is impossible to explain except through the lens of race."

The Washington Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs represented the NAACP.

"The court acknowledged that such names inflict real, racially disproportionate harm," said Kaitlin Banner, deputy legal director.

The Virginia NAACP filed the suit on behalf of six students and their parents in June 2024 after the school board voted 5-1 to change Mountain View High School back to Stonewall Jackson High School and Honey Run Elementary back to Ashby-Lee Elementary, which combines the names of Gen. Robert E. Lee and Turner Ashby, a Confederate cavalry officer. The board reversed a 2020 decision to remove the original names against a backdrop of nationwide protests over racial injustice.

The NAACP argued in its lawsuit that Black students, who make up less than 3% of the school system's population, would be "required against their will to endorse the violent defense of slavery pursued by the Confederacy and the symbolism that these images have in the modern White supremacist movement."

Under President Donald Trump's second administration, some statues honoring Confederate figures have been restored after being removed in 2020. It is part of Trump's ongoing efforts to control how American history is framed at Smithsonian museums, monuments in national parks and in classrooms.

Board members who voted to restore the Confederate names said they were honoring popular community sentiment. They said the previous board members who voted to remove the names in 2020 had ignored constituents and due process on the matter.

title: After blowing through its entire 2026 AI budget in months, Uber CTO says, ‘We’re coming to the end of the so-called tokenmaxxing era’
description: “You might expect costs to rise as adoption accelerates,” Praveen Neppalli Naga said. “We’ve seen the opposite.”
fullText:
Uber believes it's found a solution to its AI spending problem after it blew through its budget for the technology in just the first few months of the year.

In an interview with The Information earlier this year, Uber chief technology officer Praveen Neppalli Naga admitted he went "back to the drawing board" on allotted spending after the rideshare giant encouraged employees to use its tools, particularly Anthropic's Claude Code, as much as possible, even devising "leaderboards" to rank software engineers on their usage.

What is Jevons paradox in AI token spending?

How did Uber solve its AI spending budget problem?

What is tokenmaxxing and why are companies backing off?

Are companies seeing ROI from their AI investments yet?

The blitz was part of a trend in "tokenmaxxing," or companies incentivizing workplace AI use, only for many to back off from the practice as they found it wasn't offering the returns on investment to justify the rapid spending. While Uber was no exception, Naga said the company has now figured out a better way to deploy AI without breaking the bank.

"We're seeing some very interesting trends on AI costs," he wrote in an X post on Wednesday. "I think it's another signal that we're coming to the end of the so-called tokenmaxxing era."

Uber quadrupled the number of employees who use frontier AI tools, Naga explained, which brought down the cost per token. It was able to do this by improving prompt caching, as well as adjusting its default model setting, evaluating new models for efficiency, and allowing engineers to see their AI usage and costs per hour.

"You might expect costs to rise as adoption accelerates," Naga continued. "We've seen the opposite. Not because we've restricted access, but because we've treated efficiency as an engineering problem rather than a budget problem."

The stakes are increasing for companies to deliver on their massive AI investments. Last month, Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank Research Institute's global head of macro and thematic research, warned AI productivity gains were still years away.

Profit margins for the Magnificent Seven swelled from 15% to 25% between the first quarters of 2023 to 2026, while the rest of the S&P 500 index saw only 10% margin growth over the same period, indicating little widespread returns on investment in AI outside of the immediate tech sector.

As of May, Uber was still trying to unlock the innovation AI promised.

"That link is not there yet," Uber president and chief operating officer Andrew Macdonald said in an interview on the Rapid Response podcast at the time. "Maybe implicitly there's more that is getting shipped, but it's very hard to draw a line between one of those stats and 'Okay, now we're actually producing like 25% more useful consumer features.'"

title: Saudi Arabia turns to Muslim military heavyweights in landmark defense pact as Iran war closes in
description: Saudi Arabia has drawn two of the Muslim world’s most formidable military powers into its defense as the Iran war moves closer to the kingdom.
fullText:
Saudi Arabia has drawn two of the Muslim world's most formidable military powers into its defense as the Iran war moves closer to the kingdom.

Pakistan and Turkey signed a NATO-style mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia in Mecca on Friday, consolidating their longstanding security ties into a collective-defense alliance that stipulates an attack against any of them "shall be regarded as attack on them all."

That commitment could draw Pakistan and Turkey into a war they have carefully kept at arm's length.

The official rationale for the agreement is "to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression" and further provide "for the enhancement of all aspects of defence cooperation among the three states," according to a statement released by all three countries.

More specifically, the pact gives Saudi Arabia a powerful new layer of protection beyond its longstanding security partnership with the United States amid growing regional doubts over whether Washington can still be relied upon to protect its oil-rich Gulf allies.

Turkey has the second-largest military in NATO, behind only the US, while Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim nation.

Such powerful allies strengthen Saudi deterrence and present a united Sunni-led military front against a mounting Iranian threat, though a Turkish official told CNN the agreement isn't directed against any specific actor and the Saudi foreign ministry insisted this "does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc."

Other regional countries can also join, the Turkish official added, raising the prospect of the alliance drawing in new members much like NATO.

The statement ⁠did not give specifics on the commitments each had accepted, and it is unclear how far the agreement would bind the three countries to any particular military action in each other's defence.

The pact also comes as Israel expands its military reach across the region and Riyadh's relations with the neighboring United Arab Emirates fray.

Pakistan and Turkey each share a border with Iran and both have strong reasons to prevent the conflict from spiraling. Pakistan must manage its sizeable Shiite population and its sensitive relationship with Tehran, while Turkey and Iran share concerns over Kurdish separatism despite competing elsewhere in the region.

Tehran repeatedly struck targets in Saudi Arabia during the war, including civilian infrastructure, energy facilities and US interests. Direct Iranian attacks on Saudi Arabia largely subsided after an April 8 ceasefire took hold, but Iran-backed groups in Yemen and Iraq continued targeting the kingdom.

Riyadh has been one of the war's most vocal opponents and has worked to restrain US President Donald Trump from escalating against the Islamic Republic. Yet the attacks Saudi Arabia continues to face from multiple fronts have left officials increasingly alarmed and frustrated.

A Saudi official told CNN on Thursday that the kingdom was bracing for a major, coordinated assault by Iran-backed militias in Iraq and Yemen, supported by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. CNN has also reported that Tehran warned Gulf nations that renewed US attacks would trigger retaliation against energy or desalination facilities across the region.

The treaty signed in Mecca on Friday therefore serves as a warning to Tehran: another major attack on Saudi Arabia could invoke the pact, draw Pakistan and Turkey into the conflict and dramatically widen the war.

Reaction emerging from Tehran indicated their dissatisfaction toward the agreement, as a senior Iranian official warned that it will not guarantee Saudi Arabia's security.

"The Saudis should understand that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan will not bring them security, just as decades of one-sided dependence on the Americans failed to do so," Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the Iranian parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said on X.

The agreement solidifies deepening military ties between these nations. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a formal mutual defense pact last September, even before Iran started directly striking Saudi sites,

CNN's Issy Ronald, Aida Karimi, Gul Tuysuz and Sophia Saifi contributed reporting.

title: Reflecting Pool issues: Why are past administrations now being blamed?

title: Taiwan’s leader boards armored vehicle to escape mock ‘decapitation strike’
description: Taiwan’s president and top officials late Wednesday practiced how they would respond to an attempted “decapitation strike,” an operation to take out the island’s leadership, like the US capture of Ven...
fullText:
Taiwan's president and top officials late Wednesday practiced how they would respond to an attempted "decapitation strike," an operation to take out the island's leadership, like the US capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro earlier this year.

An armored personnel carrier whisked President Lai Ching-te and members of his staff from their offices in the capital Taipei to a fortified command center near the Defense Ministry, a statement from the president's office said.

"The drill was intended to review the command structure, inter-agency coordination, and emergency-response mechanisms, so as to ensure that the government can continue operating effectively and safeguarding national security" during any possible action against the island, Karen Kuo, the presidential spokesperson, said in a statement on Thursday.

A government handout video showed the armored vehicle speeding through Taipei streets on the way to the command center. Lai was also seen donning a flak jacket, listening to briefings and issuing instructions during the drill.

Dubbed the "Wan Chun," the drill was part of the 10-day Han Kuang exercises, the island's largest annual military drills, which began on Wednesday.

The Wan Chun drill simulates the evacuation of Taiwan's leader to a safe place in the event of war or other emergencies.

While it was the first known time for Lai to participate, previous leaders like Tsai Ing-wen and Ma Ying-jeou have done so. It's been around since the Cold War era, when then leader Chiang Kai-shek became wary of an attempt on the island by the Chinese Communist Party, which claims Taiwan as part of its sovereign territory, despite never having controlled it.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping has vowed to bring Taiwan under party's control, and has not ruled out the use of force to do so.

Meanwhile, Beijing keeps almost constant pressure on the democratic island with its own military exercises and gray-zone activities, tactics employing non-military assets like law enforcement and administrative units, in areas surrounding the island.

But the global security situation has brought new urgency to the Taiwanese exercises this year.

The US capture of Maduro in early January and the US-Israeli decapitation strikes on Tehran's leadership in the early stages of the war against Iran have demonstrated a need for prudent preparation.

"Taiwan needs to ready itself for the scenario now unfolding in Iran – and fast," Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at Australia's Lowy Institute's Foreign Policy and Public Opinion Program, wrote in March.

A senior Taiwan defense official told reporters ahead of the drills that they are no longer a "lab-like exercise in a vacuum."

Late Thursday night, Taiwanese troops practiced defending the Danjiang Bridge at a critical chokepoint that could give Chinese forces a shortcut to capture Taipei, as annual war games entered their second day of testing the island's ability ‌to repel an attack.

The nearly one-kilometer-long bridge, which opened earlier this year, hovers above the Tamsui River, potentially giving adversaries direct entry to the heart of Taipei. The area is considered strategically significant for its proximity to the Taipei port and beaches in Taiwan that could serve as a valuable staging area for the Chinese military.

To simulate thwarting advances by enemy forces using the bridge, soldiers erected layers of barriers and rolled barbed wire.

During the first two days of the island's largest war games, some 20,000 reservists were mobilized to practice the defense of critical infrastructure such as ports, power plants and bridges. Air defense missile systems like the Patriots and Tien-Kung could also be seen on the streets in downtown Taipei.

Next week, for the first time ever, Taiwan will deliberately slow its mobile internet speed, testing how citizens would communicate if bandwidth becomes scarce in emergencies ranging ⁠from disasters to a Chinese invasion.

title: New video shows gunman shooting victims at Idaho In-N-Out Burger drive-thru

fullText:
Police released video Friday of a mass shooting that killed three people at an Idaho In-N-Out Burger, and praised an employee from a nearby store who engaged the gunman outdoors, slowing him down and possibly preventing more deaths as authorities were catching up.

The story of heroism told by police for the first time adds to the list of at least three more people who confronted the gunman with their own weapons as well as numerous others who rushed to comfort victims.

"What happened here was violent, frightening and deeply traumatic," Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said during a news conference.

The video revealed more details of the chaotic scene last weekend. The gunman walked up to the drive-thru window four times and opened fire, killing an In-N-Out employee, police said.

Ten people were shot — inside the restaurant, directly outside, on an adjacent busy road and at a car charging station in a Twin Falls visitors center lot, Hicks said.

He said investigators still don't have a motive for the shooting. The gunman, Chad Williams, 24, killed himself.

It should have been a "normal Saturday afternoon," Hicks said. "Employees showing up for work. Visitors coming to see our beautiful city. Instead they were confronted with chaos, fear and now loss."

As the shooting unfolded, employees from nearby stores fled to a walking trail. When the gunman headed to the trail, he came across two people, including one with his hands in the air talking to him, according to the video.

That man distracted the gunman from possibly pursuing others on the trail. Williams subsequently killed himself as police closed in. His body was found near a canyon.

"To that young man, you are a hero," Hicks said. "Your courage, your composure, your selflessness in that moment likely gave others the time they needed to escape harm. This community is grateful for you, and we will never forget what you did that day."

Hicks also praised the work of an off-duty state trooper, who shot at Williams from inside the restaurant, and former police officer A.J. James, who was wounded while confronting him. Authorities previously credited an armed civilian who fired back and diverted Williams from the restaurant.

James ran toward the sound of gunfire from the drive-thru window, while the off-duty officer inside the In-N-Out exchanged gunfire with Williams through the window and directed workers out of the building, Hicks said.

He acted "heroically and unbelievably" to try to slow down the shooter, the police chief said, declining to release the off-duty officer's name.

Braxton Steube said he was the person who encountered Williams on the trail after fleeing a Dick's Sporting Good store.

"I said, 'I have a family.' I said, 'You don't have to do this. I'll tell you whatever you want. I'll do anything,'" Steube told KMVT-TV. "He started to like tear up a bit, it seemed. And he said to me, 'Just get away from me, man.'"

Steube said the gunman shot at him and missed.

The Twin Falls In-N-Out, 130 miles (210 kilometers) southeast of Boise, the state capital, had opened in July as part of the chain's expansion into Idaho.

Police identified those killed as Ashley Garibay, 23, of Stockton, California; Dale Schultz, 66, of Salt Lake City; and Christopher Claunch, 59, of Hagerman, Idaho.

Williams had briefly attended the College of Southern Idaho and previously lived in Arizona.

title: San Francisco dad questioned by park rangers for teaching his own kids tennis at public court
description: Sam Dogen says San Francisco park rangers asked whether he had a tennis permit while he was practicing with his two children on a public court.
fullText:
A California father says he simply wanted to spend an afternoon playing tennis with his children but instead found himself being questioned by park rangers who believed he was illegally teaching lessons without a permit.

Sam Dogen, a San Francisco father of two, told Fox News Digital he was practicing with his 6-year-old daughter and 9-year-old son at Golden Gate Heights Park after returning from a family trip to Hawaii.

"I took the kids out for what I thought would be a nice afternoon ... to get over the jet lag, be outside in the sun and go play some tennis like we've done many, many times," Dogen said.

About 20 minutes into their practice session, Dogen said two San Francisco Recreation and Parks Department rangers approached and asked whether he had a permit to teach tennis.

Cannabis Cafes May Become Tourist Draw In Us City As Lung Experts Cite 'Toxic Chemical' Concerns

"I was immediately thinking to myself, 'What are you talking about? These are my kids,'" he recalled.

According to Dogen, the confusion ended only after one of his children spoke up.

"He's my daddy," his son told the rangers, Dogen said.

The family was never cited, but Dogen said one ranger told him the penalty for teaching without a permit could have been $192.

Moderate San Francisco Mayor's 'Political Machine' Indicates The City's Shift To The Center: Report

Dogen emphasized that the encounter ended with what he described as an educational warning, not a citation. Still, he questioned why the interaction happened at all.

"There was nobody waiting," he said. "It was just a surprise to me. Why even bother trying to disrupt a perfectly nice afternoon, father with his children?"

The Recreation and Parks Department previously told The San Francisco Standard that rangers routinely check whether people providing instruction on public courts are operating commercially, since paid tennis instruction requires a permit.

"This was a routine interaction," department spokesperson Tamara Aparton told the outlet. "Because paid instruction is not allowed on public courts without a permit, rangers will sometimes ask questions to determine whether someone is providing commercial instruction or simply using the courts for personal recreation or coaching their kids."

San Francisco Judge Not Convinced Reparations Fund Will Be Discriminatory During Lawsuit Hearing

Dogen said he understands why the city regulates commercial instruction but added that he believes parents teaching their own children should be treated differently.

"Raising children in a city as expensive as San Francisco is hard enough," Dogen told Fox News Digital. "When you add law enforcement officers who aren't friendly, it gets even tougher."

He said his immediate concern during the interaction was making sure the situation stayed calm with his children standing nearby.

"My only instinct was to de-escalate and keep my 6-year-old daughter and 9-year-old son safe," Dogen said.

Looking ahead, Dogen joked that he may carry documentation with him the next time he takes his children to the public courts.

"I'm going to get their birth certificates and carry them with me in my tennis bag just to prove they're my children," he said. "I'm not going to get a permit to teach my children."

Dogen said he hopes the incident prompts city officials to take a more family-friendly approach to enforcing park rules.

"My hope is that San Francisco becomes a more welcoming place for children and families, not a place where a father teaching his own kids tennis on an empty court gets threatened with a $192 fine," he said.

In the documentary clip from 2020, which resurfaced in a story by The Midwesterner Friday, El-Sayed walks through Michigan's Mackinac Island during his failed run for governor.

"I hate Mackinac so much," El-Sayed said of one of the state's most recognizable vacation spots, which sits on an island in Lake Huron between Michigan's Upper and Lower peninsula's.

"I'm just gonna be like every time I've ever come here. I've hated it. Why am I here?"

The clip went viral on social media Thursday with conservatives blasting El-Sayed for looking down on the quaint village town.

"The rising stars of the Democrat Party loathe America and seek to destroy it," Federalist editor-in-chief Mollie Hemingway posted on X. "And unlike their spiritual forebears, they see less of a reason to hide it for political gain. "

"I got engaged on this island," Outkick founder Clay Travis posted on X. "It's an awesome place. Honestly, I don't understand how anyone could hate northern Michigan in summer, absolutely beautiful, most underrated spot in the country."

Apple Just Added These New Android Devices to Its Trade-In List
description: The company also increased the trade-in values for some Apple devices.
fullText:
It's a weird time to be shopping for new tech. On the one hand, "RAMageddon" is making devices more expensive and harder to find; on the other, companies are trying new tactics to get you to buy new stuff more frequently. Take Apple: While it might be more difficult than ever to buy a MacBook Air from the company, Apple will now let you "lease" new products for one-, two-, or three-year agreements. Sure, Macs and iPads might cost more than ever, but you might find it easier to pay those prices over 24 or 36 months, interest-free.

Each device's payment plan is presented without a trade-in in mind, but you can apply a trade-in if you choose to lease. Apple will lower your payments based on the value of the device you hand over at the time of signing. The better the value of your device, the lower your payments will be. What's especially interesting given the current tech market is that Apple seems to be sweetening the pot for customers with trade-ins, which will likely only push more towards this "Apple Upgrade" program.

As reported by 9to5Mac, Apple just increased its trade-in values for a number of products. Most of these are Apple's own devices. The company bumped up the trade-in values of many iPhones, Apple Watches, iPads, and Macs, some more than others. You can now get up to $70 more for your iPhone 16 Pro than you could before, or up to $20 more for your iPhone 13 Pro Max. The actual amount depends on the device in question, and the condition you bring it to Apple in.

If you're trading in a Mac, the numbers are definitely more significant. Apple bumped some models' trade-in values up over $100, and increased Mac Studio values by $260. That said, other values were much smaller: You can only get another $25 for your iMacs, and Apple didn't change the $315 maximum for your iMac Pro.

Equally noteworthy, however, is that Apple has expanded the list of Android devices eligible for trade-in values too. If you're looking to switch from Android to iPhone, there's a good chance Apple will give you some money towards a new purchase or lease.

New this week are the Galaxy S21 Ultra 5G, Google Pixel 9 Pro XL, Google Pixel 9 Pro, Google Pixel 9, OnePlus 13, and OnePlus 13R. title: 10 Screenshot Hacks Every Mac User Should Know
description: You don't need to remember multiple keyboard shortcuts.
fullText:
While third-party screenshot apps are excellent on the Mac, Apple has steadily improved its default tools. Today, the Mac's built-in screenshot utility is good enough for most people. You can, of course, use it to take screenshots, but you can do so much more, such as record a video of your screen, or even create professional screencasts. If you find yourself taking screenshots on your Mac, these are the 10 best hacks you need to know.

I find I only need to save around 10% of the screenshots I take. Left to its default settings, my Mac would save the other 90%, adding to an endless clutter I'd never take care of. As such, I always save screenshots to my Mac's clipboard, so I can paste it in the app of my choice without saving the image at all. Goodbye clutter. On your Mac, you can do this by using two keyboard shortcuts. Press Command-Control-Shift-3 for a screenshot of the entire screen, or use Command-Control-Shift-4 to capture an area of your screen. You can then paste these screenshots in any app or social media site.

Not only do I use these shortcuts exclusively, I've actually disabled the shortcuts to save screenshots to the Mac because I basically never use them. If you want to do the same, click the Apple logo in the top-left corner of your Mac's screen, and go to System Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts > Screenshots. Here, disable "Save picture of screen as a file" and "Save picture of selected area as a file."

If you are going to save screenshots to your Mac, you don't have to live with Apple's defaults. When you take screenshots on the Mac, the default save location is the desktop. This piles up fast. To avoid this mess, press Command-Shift-5, and go to Options > Other Location…. You can choose a folder or create a new one for your screenshots. Once you create this folder, you can open Finder, and drag it to the Trash side of the Dock for quick access.

Your Mac allows you to capture screenshots of a single window. After you hit Command-Shift-4, you can press the Spacebar key. This will turn your cursor into a camera icon, and you can click any open app to take a screenshot of the active window. When you view the screenshot, you'll notice that macOS adds a shadow effect on all sides, along with a transparent border. However, if you want a more tightly framed screenshot, you can eliminate the shadow with a hidden shortcut.

To do this, press Command-Shift-4, hit Spacebar, and hold down the Option key while clicking an app window. You'll have to hit Option every time you want to remove the shadow, however. If you want to make shadow-free screenshots the default, you'll have to run the following command in Terminal:

defaults write com.apple.screencapture disable-shadow -bool true; killall SystemUIServer

To restore defaults, you can simply replace "true" with "false" in the Terminal command and run it again.

Keyboard shortcuts are great, but they're not necessarily easy to remember—especially for the many screenshot options on macOS. Fortunately, Apple allows you to add the Screenshot utility to your Mac's Dock. To add it open Finder on your Mac, go to the Applications folder, then scroll down and open the Utilities folder. You can now drag the Screenshot tool to the Dock for one-click access.

If there's one screenshot keyboard shortcut to remember, it's Command-Shift-5. This key combination reveals all the screenshot options you need and doesn't leave any room for guesswork about what your screenshot tool is actually doing. It shows a floating toolbar with screenshot tools, screen recording tools, and multiple capture and record options. It's slower than using Apple's various keyboard shortcuts, but I can't argue against having all options available in a single window, so I always recommend this keyboard shortcut for those who are new to screenshots on Mac.

If you're trying to take a screenshot of something timely or quick, it's easy to miss the moment. Instead of trying to hit the button at just the right time, you can set a delay of five to 10 seconds to set up a screenshot or a screen recording, and avoid retakes. To set this up, press Command-Shift-5, and go to Options. Under the Timer section, you can choose your delay timing.

I generally like to hide the mouse pointer from screenshots and screen recordings, but when my parents need help with a Mac-related issue, showing mouse clicks in screen recordings helps. That way, they can see my cursor and all of my clicks, so they can follow along. You can enable this by pressing Command-Shift-5, clicking Options, and selecting Show mouse clicks.

Your Mac's Screenshot tool lets you record your screen with microphone audio, and even supports external mics. Pair this with a five to 10-second delay in starting the recording, and you can create screencasts with audio in one go. To use this feature, press Command-Shift-5, select any of the screen recording options, click Options, and select your mic from the Microphone section.

The iPhone ships with a great screen recording tool, but iOS doesn't allow you to record everything on your phone. In addition, some apps block screenshots and screen recordings. If you need to bypass these restrictions, you can try using a Mac to record your iPhone's screen. The easiest method is to use the iPhone Mirroring app that ships with your Mac. You can connect the iPhone wirelessly to your Mac, and use the macOS Screenshot tool instead.

QuickTime Player offers another way to do this, but you'll need to plug your iPhone into your Mac using a USB cable. Open QuickTime Player, and go to File > New Movie Recording to get started. Click the down-arrow button next to the record button, and select your iPhone to start recording.

Your Mac takes high-quality screenshots by default, and it uses the PNG format for these images. The drawback is file sizes, and especially on newer Macs with high-resolution displays, you can end up with dozens of megabytes per screenshot. If these screenshots are taking up too much space on your Mac, you can use the following Terminal command to switch the default screenshot format to JPG.

defaults write com.apple.screencapture type jpg; killall SystemUIServer

Be aware that this will significantly reduce the quality of your screenshots, and in particular, it may make text illegible in these images. If that's bothering you, then you can restore PNG screenshots by replacing "jpg" with "png" in the command mentioned above.

title: Five Ways to Make Gemini Behave More Like Google Assistant
description: If Google Assistant is headed for the graveyard, let's at least try to save what we can.
fullText:
Google Assistant is about to get one heck of a headstone in the Google Graveyard. The voice assistant has been a handy tool for years, but the company has finally decided to replace it with Gemini entirely. If you’re not exactly thrilled about the AI-ification of every app you use, there are a few ways to make Gemini behave a bit more like the Assistant of yore.

The switch from Assistant has been coming for a while; it’s a seismic shift for a lot of devices. On top of deprecating Assistant on Android phones and tablets, it’s also disappearing for Wear OS devices and some Android Auto cars. Some smart home devices and TVs will still support Assistant, but you can switch to Gemini (and you might want to since the choice is likely to be made for you eventually).

Regardless of how you feel about AI chatbots, using Gemini might become unavoidable if you’re in the Google ecosystem. So, if you want to keep the functionality you had in your phone, car, or kitchen, it might take a little bit of effort. Here’s how to get started.

When September rolls around, you’re going to be pushed to Gemini on your Google-powered phone, tablet, and watch, but that might not cover all your devices. If you’re going to be reprogramming your muscle memory, you may as well do it all at once.

Depending on when you set up your Google Home or Nest devices, you might’ve gotten a prompt to upgrade to Gemini. If not, open the Google Home app, tap your profile picture, and choose “Home settings.” Here, you should find a banner that lets you set up Gemini for Home.

It might sound counterintuitive to move away from Assistant in order to make Gemini work more like Assistant, but in the next sections I’ll walk through how to rebuild your favorite Assistant commands. This step will make the whole system work more consistently, but activating Gemini on your smart speakers is technically optional. Just be aware that if you opt not to do this, you might hit some bumps if your phone and smart speaker try to compete to respond to your commands with different assistants.

Part of the appeal of Google Assistant was its simplicity. Turn your lights on and off, set reminders, stuff like that. No trying to plan your meals for you based on your travel itinerary and anime viewing history or whatever. If that kind of simplicity appeals to you, consider taking the opposite of our previous advice, and turn off many of the “Connected Apps” you find there.

In the Gemini app on your phone, you can find this under Settings > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps. Here, you’ll find a list of apps you can connect (or disconnect) to affect how Gemini responds. You might want to turn off some of these to simplify your assistant’s responses, like Google Workspace or Search Services. These use data connected to your Google account to personalize your results, which might muck up what you’re trying to accomplish.

However, some of these apps should probably stay on. Google Home, for example, is used to control your smart home devices, and Utilities handles things like timers and alarms. Other functions are, in typical Google fashion, a bit convoluted. Reminders, for example, are typically handled by Google apps like Tasks (or sometimes Keep or Calendar?) so you might want to keep Workspace enabled, depending on your needs.

I’ve been singing the praises of this feature for a while, but if you’re frustrated with how Gemini behaves, the most powerful tool to bend it to your will is the Instructions for Gemini (previously Saved Info) tool. While ostensibly this is used to store information about yourself that you want Gemini to keep in mind, you can use it to create custom shorthand commands that work a lot more like how Assistant used to.

To access this, head to Settings > Personal Intelligence > Instructions for Gemini in the Gemini app. Here, you can add custom instructions in natural language. So, for example, let’s say you want to turn off the living room and kitchen lights with a short command, you could add the following instructions: “If a prompt consists solely of ‘good night’, turn off the lights in the living room and kitchen.” You can further tailor this command to make sure it works reliably.

This can also be a handy way to make sure that Gemini uses the right app or tool for the commands you want to run. For example, if you want to add a note to your Google Keep app, but Gemini keeps trying to set reminders via the Tasks app or whatever, you can add custom instructions to “Always use Keep to store notes and reminders” so your future commands work the way you want them to.

Google Assistant’s routines feature has moved around over the years, and it currently lives in the Google Home app. But in keeping with Google’s long-standing strategy of “build two of everything”, you can also use Gemini’s scheduled actions to replace some of this functionality. While it’s not strictly necessary, as long as Google Home automations exist, it can be easier to do everything from the one app you’re being pushed into anyway. Especially if you’re worried that the older method will suddenly be removed.

In the Gemini app, head to Settings > Scheduled actions, and tap New Action. Here you can give your routine a name, describe what you want Gemini to do in the same natural language you can use for other Gemini commands. You can also set a time and frequency you want the action to occur.

Gemini works a little differently than Assistant, so some of these commands might not run with as much precision as you’re used to. Gemini notes in the app that scheduled actions are prepared up to an hour in advance, so keep that in mind. This tool can be handy for things like a morning routine, giving you a morning briefing at the same time as turning on your lights. But if you want very simple actions—like, say, just turning on the lights—you might still want to use the automations in the Google Home app.

One of the biggest annoyances with the forced switch to Gemini is that commands can take a lot longer to process. Recognizing a few key words like “turn on lights” is fast. Trying to process whole sentences is more complicated. If you preferred the speed of Assistant and don’t need more complex analysis of your instructions, changing your model can help.

In most cases, you can’t change the default Gemini model (Google, please), but in the Gemini app, you can tap the model dropdown and choose whatever the latest, lightest model is. At time of writing, that’s 3.5 Flash-Lite, but it may be different later. Typically, the fastest model will be whichever one has the oldest version number, paired with words like “Flash” or “Lite”.

You can also find an optional toggle labeled “Extended thinking” which usually attempts more complex processing. But it also adds extra processing time, dragging out simple commands like setting alarms. Disable this, and you’ll typically get faster answers. Depending on how you invoke Gemini, you might not have the option to tweak your models, but when you can, you can find a pretty significant speed boost by making these changes.

title: Lammonby helps revive Somerset's One-Day Cup hopes
description: Somerset keep their hopes of qualifying for the latter stages of the One-Day Cup alive with a thumping victory over Surrey, thanks to a brilliant Tom Lammonby ton.
fullText:
Somerset kept their hopes of qualifying for the latter stages of the One-Day Cup alive with a thumping victory over Surrey, thanks to a brilliant Tom Lammonby ton.

The opener hit 114 in a huge partnership with captain Lewis Goldsworthy as Somerset thrashed their Group A rivals.

Elsewhere, Leicestershire pipped Warwickshire to stay top of the group, while Luc Benkenstein's electric innings of 140 helped Essex edge past Glamorgan in a Cardiff nail-biter.

Middlesex remain top of Group B after a tight victory over Durham who lost England international Emilio Gay to injury early in his innings.

And holders Worcestershire Rapids chased down 334 at lowly Sussex in the penultimate over, directed beautifully by captain Jake Libby with an unbeaten century.

At Chesterfield, Northamptonshire reached 259-8 from their 50 overs thanks to contributions from opener Luke Proctor (53), captain Nathan McSweeney (49) and George Bartlett (55).

It became increasingly apparent, though, that the visitors were short as Nottinghamshire's chase wore on, despite losing opener Ben Martindale for 18 and Tayyab Tahir for eight.

At 64-2, Freddie McCann then hit 91 before being trapped by Yuzvendra Chahal while captain Haseeb Hameed added a knock of 51 to place the hosts in a position of strength.

Kyle Verreynne (39 not out) and Lyndon James (45 not out) then put on an unbroken partnership of 69 to steer Notts to a comfortable six-wicket victory with more than three overs to spare.

Having lost Johnny Connell cheaply, Somerset pair Lammonby (114) and Goldsworthy (83) blitzed 152 from 141 deliveries for the second wicket to set up the hosts' big 188-run victory over Surrey at Taunton.

Middle order pair Archie Vaughan (52) and Kian Roberts (32) built on that early partnership as Somerset posted a mammoth 368-9.

Surrey's pursuit got off to the worst possible start when they lost Dominic Sibley for a two-ball duck and fellow top-order batters Ryan Patel (40), Rory Burns (15) and Adam Thomas (9) soon followed to leave the visitors flailing at 65-4.

Ollie Sykes (34) and Josh Blake (47) shared a 57-run partnership to drag Surrey back into the equation, but the visitors were bowled out for 180.

Leicestershire continued their march towards qualification as they sealed a three-wicket victory over Warwickshire at Grace Road.

The Bears were in trouble at 31-4, but young pair Kai Smith (57) and Vansh Jani (33) stemmed the flow of wickets and began to drag the visitors back into the contest.

Smith and George Garton (38) put on 68 before both departed in the space of two balls as Leicestershire cleaned up the tail and the Bears were left to defend 220.

Oliver Hannon-Dalby (3-27) led the charge as Warwickshire made scoring runs for Leicestershire especially difficult in the early stages.

But the hosts recovered from 10-3 and then 43-4 to claim victory thanks to the calm and measured presence of Nick Kelly with a quality knock of 86.

Cameron Bancroft fell just two short of a century for Gloucestershire as they suffered a four-wicket defeat by Lancashire in the penultimate over of the match at Old Trafford - a result which keeps the hosts' hopes of qualifying alive.

Gloucestershire captain Jack Taylor supported Australian opener Bancroft with a contribution of 75 which pushed his side up to 270-6.

Lancashire's top order, in reply, laid the foundations for a successful chase. Matty Hurst was bowled by Aman Rao for 48, while Josh Bohannon hit 42 before he was caught and bowled by Ed Middleton.

The experienced Keaton Jennings made a reliable 67, but when middle-order pair Rocky Flintoff and Harry Singh departed cheaply, there remained work to do for the Red Rose at 183-6.

George Balderson (56 not out) and Arav Shetty (36 not out) saw Lancashire home late in the game with an unbroken 61-ball stand of 90.

Middlesex clinched their fifth win of the competition with a brilliantly measured chase to add insult to injury for Durham, who had England opener Gay retire hurt earlier in the day.

Durham posted 303 from their 50 overs and, although Gay left the field unable to continue with a shoulder complaint on nine, his opening partner Alex Lees added 103. Will Rhodes also contributed 65, while Middlesex bowler Naavya Sharma claimed figures of 4-64 from his 10 overs.

Chasing a daunting target, Middlesex put runs on the board early.

When Josh De Caires (34) got out to Kasey Aldridge, Middlesex captain Ben Geddes (77) and Joe Cracknell (84) immediately picked up the baton and put on 96 for the third wicket.

Neither were there to steer Middlesex over the line, but late hitting from tail-enders Toby Roland-Jones and Henry Brookes finished the job with just three balls left.

Yorkshire all-but sealed progress from Group B with a five-wicket win over Derbyshire at Scarborough, thanks to substantial contributions from batters James Wharton and Sam Whiteman.

Openers Harry Came (58) and Martin Andersson (67) shared a stand worth 140 for the Falcons before the hosts fought back.

Ben Cliff (3-57) led the way with the ball to ensure Derbyshire were made to settle on 278-8, and that made for an enticing out-ground chase.

Derbyshire appeared well placed to defend that figure when they had Yorkshire at 57-3. But century partnerships between Wharton (75) and Whiteman (94), and then Whiteman and George Hill (63 not out) carefully guided the hosts to victory in the final over of a gripping match.

Essex edged a thriller, winning by just three runs against hosts Glamorgan as more than 600 runs were scored and 17 wickets fell at Sophia Gardens.

Put in, Essex openers Benkenstein and Noah Thain (76) put on 166 for the first wicket, as the former smoked 140 from just 109 balls.

Having been 257-2, Essex collapsed and were bowled out for 312 with 17 deliveries left of their innings. However, they were well placed to defend that when they reduced Glamorgan to 78-5, with Shane Snater (3-49) making in-roads with the ball.

A terrific unbeaten 118 from Timm van der Gugten, well supported in the middle overs by Alex Horton (85), hauled Glamorgan towards the victory line.

Yet they fell short when needing six from the final over as Mackenzie Jones restricted them to just two.

Fynn Hudson-Prentice top scored with a blistering 68 from only 35 balls as he helped Sussex up to 333-9 - but Worcestershire Rapids won the day at Hove thanks to their skipper.

Hudson-Prentice, in his final season with Sussex before he joins Hampshire in 2027, was one of eight players in the batting order to pass 20 in a true team effort which failed to bear fruit.

Ben Gibbon (3-74) was rewarded for his efforts with the ball, but Jack Leaning also posted 50 as the hosts set an imposing total for their visitors to chase.

Isaac Mohammed (44) and Brett D'Oliveira (31) set the platform for the hunt and then Kashif Ali smashed 73 from 51 balls, including six fours and three sixes.

Libby played a captain's knock to anchor the chase, finishing on 109 not out as the Rapids chased down their target with 10 balls remaining.

title: Scotland beat Canada to reach World Cup Qualifier
description: Scotland hold on for a nervy nine-run victory over Candada to secure a place at next year's World Cup Qualifier after a tense tri-series match in Forfarshire.
fullText:
ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2 tri-series, Forthill

Scotland 281-7 (50 overs): McCreath 112; Shirzad 3-55

Canada 272 (49.2): Samra 78; McMullen 3-43

Scotland held on for a nervy nine-run victory over Candada to secure a place at next year's World Cup Qualifier after a tense ICC Cricket World Cup League 2 match in Forfarshire.

Fin McCreath's 112, his first international century, helped the hosts post 281-7 at Forthill.

Canada hit 50 inside eight overs thanks to Yuvraj Sumra (78), but they fell to 181-7 only for a partnership of 84 by Ansh Patel and captain Saad Bin Zafar to take them close to their target before George Munsey's catch secured Scotland's win with four balls remaining.

Scotland are now assured a place at next year's Qualifier as Canada cannot catch them in the League 2 standings.

It was the first game of the tri-series, which also involves the United Arab Emirates, to beat the wet weather after two washouts.

Grange batter McCreath reached his century from 135 balls in the 47th over.

title: Euro navel gazing & early troubles for Scottish title hopefuls
description: Already it is looking like the Scottish title might be won again by the best of a bad bunch, but what can we look forward to this weekend?
fullText:
It has been a tough start to the season for last term's big three in the Scottish Premiership.

Reigning champions Celtic stole a march on runners-up Heart of Midlothian and city rivals Rangers considering they won on the opening weekend, albeit by a single goal against a visiting Dundee side many are predicting will be in a relegation battle come the end of the season.

But then came the news on Wednesday that veteran manager Martin O'Neill was in hospital after undergoing what they said was "a small precedure".

On the field of play, Hearts suffered a 6-1 humiliation away to Benfica - their fourth defeat in a row already this season - while Rangers followed up their 1-1 draw away to Dundee United by also losing in the Europa League qualifiers, 2-1 away to Jagiellonia Bialystok.

Already it is looking like the Scottish title might be won again by the best of a bad bunch, but what can we look forward to this weekend?

'Critically important' summit called on future of Scottish football

Scottish summer malaise continues but some room for optimism

Dundee head coach Steven Pressley got a bit of stick for playing down his side's chances not only at Celtic Park on Monday but in the league overall.

However, that did not prevent them giving a good account of themselves against the champions and they head into Saturday's game against Aberdeen having won their latest five home games - including three in the top flight.

Having failed to beat the Dons in their previous 33 meetings, they have also won the latest two between the sides.

In saying that, they will be wary of a Dons side who have scored at least twice against them in each of their latest seven league meetings.

It is also an Aberdeen side that have been improving since Stephen Robinson took charge and, after their opening defeat of Hearts, have won four of their latest Premiership games, with only Celtic having won more points since April.

Two other sides who started with a win - St Mirren and promoted St Johnstone - meet in Paisley, where the visiting Saints will be looking to start a Premiership season with two victories for the first time since 2017.

Sunday navel gazing after a bruising midweek in Europe is becoming all too familiar for Scottish football, but this time Motherwell and Hibernian can look forward to second legs with some real hopes of progress, albeit in the third-tier Conference League qualifiers.

The Lanarkshire side will hope to finish off the job after a 1-1 draw away to HJK Helskini as they continue to earn plaudits for the style of play adopted last season by Jens Berthel Askou and adapted by new manager Alfred Johansson.

However, they will have to improve first on their record against Falkirk, who have won on their latest three visits to Fir Park and have not lost to Well in six meetings.

Since a 1-0 win over Well at Falkirk Stadium in May, though, John McGlynn's side have lost four in a row in the Premiership.

Hibs' 2-1 win over North Macedonians Shkendija was a bit of struggle, but at least it was better than their opening defeat at home to Well.

Now they travel to Glasgow looking to become the first-ever side to win in consecutive league games at Ibrox after winning 2-1 there in May.

Indeed, Hibs have won on two of their last three league visits and another would heap more pressure on new Rangers manager Derek McInnes after Thursday's defeat in Poland.

That will be especially so should Celtic, who could be without O'Neill despite the manager being released from hospital, secure a ninth win in a row over Kilmarnock and a ninth league win in a row overall to create a healthy early lead over their title rivals.

The odds of that must be good considering the Ayrshire side, who lost their opener to St Johnstone, have failed to win their first two top-flight games in 12 of the previous 15 seasons.

Similarly, Hearts cannot afford a third consecutive league defeat - having lost last season's decider against Celtic then their opener with Aberdeen - if they are to mount a similar challenge to the one under McInnes last term.

They have not won on Dundee United's last three visits to Tynecastle and further questions will be asked of new head coach Wouter Vrancken if they suffer a fifth straight defeat.

The Belgian's side have lost 14 goals in those four games and will not be helped by centre-half Stuart Findlay's suspension, but United have themselves not kept a clean sheet in 17 away games in the Premiership and have kept the fewest away clean sheets of any side since the start of last season.

It could be a goal fest at Tynecastle.

Nicolas Raskin made his return from World Cup duty as a substitute for Rangers in Poland and he and fellow defensive midfielder Cammy Devlin made such a big difference after the break that both will be pushing for starts against Hibs.

Slightly further forward, though, Thelo Aasgaard remains an enigma - the Norway international having scored in his last three Rangers appearances but leaving McInnes frustrated with moments that are either laziness or misplaced arrogance.

Findlay Curtis must also be pushing for a start after the 20-year-old impressed as a substitute for new wing signing Daisuke Yokota.

Rangers are in dire need of someone like Sweden midfielder Benjamin Nygren, who scored Celtic's winner against Dundee. No player has scored more than his 17 goals - or six winners - in the Premiership since the beginning of last season.

Kevin Nisbet is also off to a flyer with a goal and assist in Aberdeen's win over Hearts and the Scotland striker will be relishing Saturday's visit to Dens Park, where he has scored his latest three away league goals.

Motherwell midfielder Lukas Fadinger has scored three goals in his latest five Premiership appearances, while St Mirren counterpart Killian Phillips' two goals against Falkirk added fuel to reports that he is being courted by clubs in Major League Soccer.

Meanwhile, former Hibs trainee Jamie Gullan marked his return to the Premiership with two assists and the forward also had more shots, chances created and touches in the opposition box than any St Johnstone player in their 4-3 win over Kilmarnock.

title: Rashid takes six wickets as Afghanistan thrash Ireland
description: Rashid Khan takes six wickets as Afghanistan beat Ireland by 92 runs in Gary Wilson's first one-day international as head coach.
fullText:
Afghanistan 299-8 (47 overs): Zadran 84 (97); Adair 2-40

Ireland 207 all out (33.4 overs): Carmichael 62 (66); Rashid 6-34

Rashid Khan took six wickets as Afghanistan beat Ireland by 92 runs in Gary Wilson's first one-day international as head coach.

After Wednesday's opener if the five-game series was washed out without a ball bowled, a wet outfield at Bready led to a 90-minute delay and a reduction of three overs per side.

Afghanistan quickly took advantage of the short boundaries at the County Tyrone ground, with a succession of batters looking set even if it was only Ibrahim Zadran who went on to pass fifty.

His 84 helped Afghanistan post 299-8 ,but Ireland could only muster 207 as Wilson's reign started with defeat.

Cade Carmichael was Ireland's top scorer with 62, but Rashid stole the show with six wickets.

The tourists have won seven ODIs against Ireland in succession, a run that stretches back to 2019.

Ireland's first ODI with Afghanistan washed out

As has been the case throughout this home summer, Ireland's bowling options were limited through injuries.

Josh Little, Matt Hollard, Craig Young and Barry McCarthy were all enforced absentees, with Wilson's first selection showing four specialist bowlers including international debutant Byron McDonough.

There was plenty of interest to see how Jai Moondra, breakout star of June's T20 series victory over India, would fare in his one-day bow with the India-born 29-year-old's two wickets coming at a cost of 78 runs.

Among that total were nine fours and three sixes with Afghanistan plundering 32 boundaries across their innings.

Seamer Mark Adair was the pick of the bunch for Ireland, even if 14 off his final over inflated his figures to 2-40.

After he signed off from The Hundred duty with figures of 5-17 for MI London on Sunday, Ireland were left wishing Rashid had seen out the season on the franchise circuit.

Back with Afghanistan, the number one-ranked ODI bowler in the world accounted for the early wickets of Andrew Balbirnie and Harry Tector, while Azmatullah Omarzai dismissed captain Paul Stirling and Carmichael.

Rashid also removed both Curtis Campher and Ben Calitz as he finished with 6-34 from 7.4 overs..

It was a disappointing start for new head coach Wilson, but Ireland have the opportunity to bounce back in the third match of the series at Stormont on Monday.

The fixtures are preparation for the 2027 World Cup qualifiers, which are set to begin next year.

title: Sunrisers claim second spot and eliminate Phoenix
description: Sunrisers Leeds move up to second in The Hundred and eliminate Birmingham Phoenix with a 45-run win at Edgbaston.
fullText:
The Hundred men's competition, Edgbaston

Sunrisers Leeds 169-7 (100 balls): Rickelton 65 (37); Tariq 2-28

Birmingham Phoenix 124-8 (100 balls): Dickson 34 (27); Carse 3-17, Potts 3-22

Sunrisers Leeds moved up to second in The Hundred and eliminated Birmingham Phoenix with a 45-run win at Edgbaston.

Opener Ryan Rickelton hit 65 from 37 balls as Sunrisers reached 169-7, while Brydon Carse and Matthew Potts took 3-17 and 3-20 respectively as Phoenix finished well short on 124-8.

South African Rickelton, who struck six fours and three sixes in his 37-ball innings, put on an opening partnership of 52 with Mitch Marsh after his side were put into bat, and then added 42 more with Harry Brook.

Off-spinner Usman Tariq took 2-28 for Phoenix, bowling the tournament's leading run-scorer Marsh for 34 and trapping England white-ball captain Brook lbw for 19.

Rickelton was run out from the 93rd ball of the innings by wicketkeeper Joe Clarke, the third of four wickets to fall for 15 runs towards the close.

Carse claimed two wickets in the Phoenix powerplay with Mitch Owen (10) and Rehan Ahmed (0) both finding fielders, the latter departing four balls after Will Smeed (9) had also been removed, caught by Rickelton off Potts.

The hosts swiftly fell behind the required run-rate, losing wickets periodically - among them Donovan Ferreira bowled for three to become Carse's third victim.

Sean Dickson top-scored for Phoenix with 34, before hitting straight to Brook in the deep off Nathan Ellis, while Potts bowled Scott Currie (5) and Tom Helm (0) with successive deliveries to extinguish any remaining hope for Phoenix.

Sunrisers moved up from fifth place, surpassing MI London and Welsh Fire on net run-rate, with Manchester Super Giants four points behind the trio of teams.

Phoenix remain bottom with one win and five losses, joining London Spirit in elimination with every team having played six games.

title: Coventry sign Ghana's Yirenkyi for record fee
description: Premier League newcomers Coventry City have completed the club-record signing of Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi.
fullText:
Premier League newcomers Coventry City have completed the club-record signing of Ghana midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi.

The 20-year-old has signed a long-term contract, with the Sky Blues believed to have paid Danish side Nordsjaelland a fee of 27m euros (£23.1m), plus 3m euros (£2.5m) in add-ons.

Yirenkyi made his international debut in May 2025 and played at this summer's World Cup, scoring a stoppage-time winner in the Black Stars' group win over Panama.

He becomes Coventry's fifth summer signing after Frank Lampard led the club back into the top flight after a 25-year absence.

"When I spoke to the head coach about the plans and the style, it's something I really like, and I look forward to learning from him," said Yirenkyi.

"I'm still young so I want to learn from the head coach, the other players and work really hard for the team."

He is a product of the Right to Dream academy and joined Nordsjaelland in 2024, winning the Danish Superliga's young player of the year award last season.

Although primarily a midfielder, Yirenkyi is known for his versatility having played at right-back for both club and country.

Danish journalist Nicklas Degn, who hosts the Mediano podcast, said Yirenkyi is an "extremely exciting player" who has been "touted as the next big thing".

Speaking to BBC Sport, he added: "He's been one of the best players in the Danish Superliga in the past season and he's extremely highly regarded.

"Everyone knew it would just be a matter of time before he went to a bigger league, especially after his World Cup.

"There's always a big focus on the young talents of Nordsjaelland. They are a club that has an academy with a talent development that has an extremely high reputation internationally.

"He's a complete number eight but his versatility is underscored by the fact he's been playing in defence for much of the spring at both Nordsjaelland and for the Ghana national team.

"Coventry will be getting their hands on a extremely exciting player who plays with a maturity well above his age group."
